Thursday, 6 August 2026
## Your pharmacist should be your first stop

#### ACT Party Leader David Seymour today released Pharmacy First – ACT's plan to get New Zealanders care without the wait by expanding what pharmacists can do and removing barriers to new pharmacies.
David Seymour
ACT Party Leader David Seymour today released Pharmacy First – ACT's plan to get New Zealanders care without the wait by expanding what pharmacists can do and removing barriers to new pharmacies.

ACT will let pharmacists treat more conditions, manage stable long-term conditions, catch cardiovascular and skin cancer risk early, cut red tape stopping new pharmacies from opening, and introduce 24-hour prescription collection through secure electronic lockers.
"In many cases, your pharmacist is the healthcare professional closest to you," Mr Seymour said. "They're trained, they're trusted, they're often available the same day.

“The rules confine pharmacists to a small number of permitted services. Meanwhile, time that pharmacists used to spend ‘counting and pouring’ is being freed up by automation, at the same time that community pharmacies are under serious revenue pressure.
“Pharmacists have the capacity, the need, and the proximity. All that's missing is permission.

"One in four adults and one in five children cannot see a GP when they need to – a figure that has more than doubled in four years. A highly qualified healthcare professional is standing right there at your local shops, ready to help. The rules just need to get out of the way.

"This policy builds on changes ACT has already delivered in Government. Pharmacists are now treating UTIs, conjunctivitis, chest infections, and ear infections. We've introduced 12-month prescriptions for stable patients, and given pharmacists prescribing rights for the first time. New Zealanders have welcomed our moves to empower pharmacists and patients, so today's announcement is the next step."
More conditions covered at your pharmacy
ACT will expand the Minor Ailments Scheme to include conditions pharmacists are trained to assess and treat:
- Throat and ENT: acute sore throat
- Skin and eyes: school sores (impetigo), stye
- Ear, nose and throat: tonsillitis and acute sore throat
- Musculoskeletal and pain: gout, osteoarthritis
- Sexual and reproductive health: vaginal thrush; chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing (self-swab kits), period pain
- Blood tests: pharmacists will be able to order appropriate blood tests directly, at a patient's request or where they identify a clinical need
A full list of ailments ACT is proposing pharmacists to treat can be found here.

"Every condition will include a clear protocol for when patients need to be referred to a GP or specialist," says Mr Seymour. "Doctors still have an important role here, but ACT will make sure that for cases a pharmacist can handle, you don't have to wait two weeks to get help."
"Consultation fees will stay capped at $20 for most patients and $5 for Community Services Card holders. The Government funds the balance."
Routine monitoring of long-term conditions

“For the roughly one million New Zealanders managing stable hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or high cholesterol, an annual GP appointment to renew the same medication is often a formality – but getting that appointment is not.

“Pharmacists already see these patients regularly, know their medicines, and are well placed to carry out routine monitoring. ACT will let accredited pharmacists provide funded annual medication reviews for stable patients, order the standard blood tests needed to monitor treatment, and adjust doses within clear, GP-set clinical limits. Anything outside those limits, or any new diagnosis, goes straight back to the patient's GP.”
Catching skin cancer sooner

“New Zealand has one of the world's highest melanoma rates, but most people must either wait for a GP or pay out of pocket to have a suspicious lesion checked. Pharmacies are often the first place people raise these concerns – there just isn't a consistent pathway for what happens next.

“ACT will allow pharmacy-based skin concern service. Trained pharmacists would record relevant risk factors and take high-quality dermatoscope images, using technology to help identify concerning changes over time. Patients who meet clear risk thresholds would be referred to a GP or specialist.
"This is not a full diagnosis service, but it would give people – especially in rural communities – a place to have a concern taken seriously and acted on quickly."
More pharmacies where you need them
"Rules that prevent new pharmacies from opening will go," says Mr Seymour.

"The five-pharmacy ownership cap – a restriction the Government's own October 2025 Regulatory Impact Statement admits is 'not being meaningfully followed' – will be explicitly removed. Proximity requirements that block new pharmacies from opening near existing ones will also go. Any pharmacy that meets safety and quality standards should be able to open.

"Pharmacy licence renewals will move from annual to five-yearly after the first year, saving pharmacists $1,000 in compliance costs each year and freeing them to focus on patients, not paperwork. Pharmacy Accuracy Checking Technicians will be allowed to transfer between pharmacies without having to sit a new course, making it easier for pharmacies, especially in smaller communities, to attract and retain staff.

"The current rules don't protect people, but they do make it harder to open pharmacies and harder to staff them. ACT's plan to empower pharmacists will create demand for more pharmacies in more communities. So, we're removing the barriers to get them there."
24-hour e-lockers

"For New Zealanders managing stable long-term conditions, ACT will enable secure prescription e-lockers – allowing patients to collect pre-dispensed medicines at any time using a digital code, similar to click-and-collect at a supermarket," says Mr Seymour.
"Lockers will not be used to dispense controlled drugs, refrigerated medicines, or medications requiring monitoring.
"This is a practical fix for rural communities where pharmacy hours are limited and collecting a prescription means a long drive at inconvenient times.

"The pharmacy network in New Zealand has enormous, untapped capacity," Mr Seymour said. "ACT is going to unlock it, so that when you're unwell, your pharmacist is the first stop. We will make life easier for Kiwis seeking basic care, and free up GPs to see patients in greater need, more quickly."
####### Law & Order
## Three Strikes for Burglary
ACT will introduce a Three Strikes for Burglary regime, requiring a minimum three-year prison sentence with no parole for anyone convicted of burglary three times.

In 2025, 184,000 New Zealanders were victims of burglary. Burglary is a recidivist crime, with the majority of people released from prison for burglary sent back to prison within two years. Nearly three-quarters are resentenced. Around one in four burglary victims have already been burgled before.
Judges keep using their leeway to give burglars more chances, and the burglars keep reoffending.
ACT says enough. If you keep breaking into people's homes, the warnings stop and real consequences kick in.

- ACT will create a new Three Strikes regime for burglary. Anyone convicted of burglary three times would receive a minimum sentence of three years in prison, with no parole, no home detention, and no early release.
- The policy would apply both to someone facing their third conviction, or to someone facing a single conviction of three or more counts of burglary.
- An aggravated burglary would trigger a strike under both this regime and the existing Three Strikes regime for violent crime.
- The judge would still retain full discretion to impose any sentence between the three-year minimum and the 10-year maximum.
Read the full policy
#### In our team’s words:
"Your home should be the one place where you feel safe," says ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee.

"It’s the place where you keep the things you've worked for, your family's memories, and the people you care about most. That sense of security should be absolute, but it’s undermined by every burglary in our neighbourhoods.

“This policy is not primarily about deterring crime. It is about preventing it. Imprisoning repeat burglars will protect New Zealanders from a small group of offenders who have shown, time after time, that they have no respect for other people's homes or property. They will not be able to victimise us from a jail cell.
"When someone does the right thing, gets up and goes to work to unlock their own potential, they shouldn’t have to worry about some deadbeat invading their home and taking their hard-earned property.
"ACT will unlock the potential of the justice system to protect victims, not make excuses for criminals.”
####### Health
## Closing the Medicines Gap
No New Zealander should have to empty their savings, uproot their family, or leave the country to access medicines Australians receive as a matter of course.

New Zealand spends just 4.9 per cent of its health budget on medicines. Australia spends 12.2 per cent, while the OECD average is 13.3 per cent. Australia funds 142 modern medicines that are not funded in New Zealand, and 38 per cent of those are cancer medicines.
Often, the medicine a patient needs is already on Pharmac's Options for Investment list. Pharmac has assessed it as worth funding, but it remains unavailable because the medicines budget has run out.

Pharmac negotiates hard and assesses which medicines will produce the greatest health gains. Then it runs out of money. Successive governments have given it a second-rate medicines budget and expected first-world results.
#### ACT will:
- Increase the share of the health budget spent on medicines by one percentage point each year, reaching parity with Australia in 2033.
- Set Pharmac's future funding increases in advance, allowing it to plan for more medicines on its Options for Investment list.
- Fund the change from expected growth in the health budget. It will not require additional taxes or reduce the size of the non-medicines health budget.
- Ask other parties to commit to the same seven-year path, so a change of government does not derail it.
Read the full policy
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Since taking responsibility for Pharmac and Medsafe, I have heard from hundreds of people whose treatment exists but is still out of reach. Often Pharmac has already assessed the medicine and put it on the Options for Investment list. The money simply is not there.

“New Zealand spends 4.9 per cent of its health budget on medicines. Australia spends 12.2 per cent. ACT would close that gap by lifting the medicines share one percentage point each year until we reach parity in 2033.

“Pharmac bargains hard and gets good value from every dollar. Governments have taken that efficiency for granted and left the budget too small. In Budget 2026, Health got an extra $1.5 billion and Pharmac got $13.5 million. Under our policy it would have received around $320 million more.”
ACT Health spokesperson Todd Stephenson says:

“Australia funds 142 modern medicines that New Zealand does not. Thirty-eight per cent are cancer medicines. Behind those figures are families draining savings, raising money, or moving overseas for treatment.

“We can close the gap without a new tax or cutting the rest of the health budget. Health spending is already growing. ACT would reserve one point of that growth for medicines each year, so more patients get treatment before they end up in hospital.”
####### Hunters and Firearms
## Open the Backcountry

Much of New Zealand’s public land is difficult to reach. In rugged country such as Fiordland, a helicopter can be the only practical way in, yet large areas remain closed by no-fly and no-landing lines with no clear conservation or safety reason.

Commercial venison recovery is also caught between DOC rules and aviation regulation. DOC can dictate the type of helicopter an operator uses even though aircraft safety is already regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority.
ACT would make access decisions clear and defensible, leave aviation safety to the aviation regulator and give hunters a proper role in balancing recreational hunting with commercial recovery.
Read the full policy
#### ACT will:
- Allow the Game Animal Council to designate sensible and accessible helicopter landing sites.
- Require DOC to use clear, public and consistent tests when deciding where aircraft may land.
- Direct the Outdoor Access Commission to make hunting access a priority in its work programme.
- Stop DOC dictating which helicopters commercial venison recovery operators can use, leaving aircraft safety to the Civil Aviation Authority.
- Allow the Game Animal Council to restrict commercial take by animal gender when necessary, so recreational hunters and recovery operators can fairly share a well-managed resource.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“Public conservation land belongs to New Zealanders, but large parts of it are effectively closed off. In country such as Fiordland, a helicopter can be the only realistic way in. Access restrictions should have a clear conservation or safety reason, not survive because of an old line on a map.
“Better access is not a licence to ignore conservation limits. It means opening the country New Zealanders already own under rules that are clear, justified and fair to the people who use it.”
ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“ACT would let the Game Animal Council identify sensible landing sites and require DOC to use a clear and public test. We would also tell the Outdoor Access Commission to prioritise hunting access when it works to secure routes onto public land.

“DOC currently makes commercial venison recovery operators use expensive turbine helicopters. Aircraft safety is the Civil Aviation Authority’s job. DOC should manage conservation effects and leave aircraft standards to the regulator established for that purpose.

“Current permits can also let commercial operators strip out the trophy stags recreational hunters value most. Where necessary, the Game Animal Council would be able to restrict take by animal gender so commercial recovery and recreational hunting can share the resource fairly.”
####### Education
## Equal Treatment at Universities
Taxpayer-funded support at university should go to students who need it. It should not be allocated according to their race.

Universities can currently reserve scholarships, accommodation, study spaces and other opportunities on the basis of ethnicity. In 2024, the Government directed public agencies to allocate support according to need and value rather than ethnicity, but tertiary institutions were not covered.

ACT's Education and Training (Equal Treatment) Amendment Bill would apply that principle to tertiary education. Universities could still support students according to academic merit, economic hardship, disability, location or a need for academic help. Privately funded scholarships and grants could still be targeted according to the donor's wishes.
#### ACT will:
- Amend the Education and Training Act to prevent tertiary institutions conferring benefits on a person or group on the basis of race or ethnic origin.
- Apply the rule to scholarships, grants, financial assistance, accommodation, designated spaces and other benefits or opportunities.
- Preserve universities' ability to allocate support according to academic merit, academic need, geographic location, economic circumstances or disability.
- Exempt endowments, bequests and other assistance provided by private individuals, iwi, charities or trusts for a targeted purpose.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Tertiary Education spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar says:

“Universities are independent, but most of their funding comes from taxpayers and legislation protects them from ordinary competition. With that privilege comes a basic obligation: taxpayer-funded opportunities should be open on equal terms.

“In 2024 the Government told public agencies to allocate services according to need and value rather than ethnicity, but universities were left outside that direction. My Bill would close that gap by applying the same principle to publicly funded tertiary institutions.

“The Bill would cover scholarships, grants, housing, designated facilities and other benefits. Universities could still recognise academic merit, provide extra academic support, respond to economic hardship or disability, and take account of where a student lives.

“Private generosity would remain private. If an iwi, charity or trust gives a university money for a scholarship aimed at Māori students, the university could continue to administer it. The change applies to the institution's own publicly funded resources: need, not race.”
####### Law & Order
## Stopping Coercion by Animal Abuse
Victims of family violence should never have to choose between their own safety and the safety of the pet they love.
Family violence isn’t just about physical abuse. Perpetrators use threats against beloved pets as another way to intimidate and trap their victims.

The evidence is confronting. Research found abusive partners were almost 11 times more likely to intentionally harm an animal than partners in non-abusive relationships. More than half of victims said they delayed leaving an abusive relationship because they felt responsible for the safety of their pets.
ACT will strengthen protections for pets used as instruments of coercion and control in family violence by:

- Amending the Crimes Act to make it an offence to use the abuse of a companion animal as a means of coercion or control in a family violence relationship, with a penalty up to seven years in imprisonment.

- Strengthening Protection Orders to ensure offenders cannot withhold, sell, give away, or otherwise dispose of a protected person's companion animal, helping keep pets with the protected person and closing a loophole exploited by family violence offenders.
- Ensuring companion animals are not left with a dangerous abuser when a Protection Order is made, reducing opportunities for offenders to use pets as a tool of coercion or control.
- Requiring Police to record pets on family harm reports to better identify risks and strengthen protections for victims and their animals.

- Giving Police explicit statutory authority and clear operational guidance to remove a companion animal to a place of safety, such as Pet Refuge or the SPCA, where they believe the animal is at risk of harm or is being used as a tool of coercion.
Read the full policy
#### In our team’s words:

"Right now, if Police attend a family violence callout, a victim may escape while the family pet is left behind with the alleged abuser. That gives offenders another way to threaten and manipulate the people they’re abusing,” says ACT’s Family and Sexual Violence spokesperson Karen Chhour.

“ACT will ensure Police have the tools they need to protect victims and remove companion animals from harm when offenders use them as weapons of coercion. New Zealand is falling behind countries that have already recognised the link between animal abuse and family violence.

"In New South Wales, harming or threatening to harm a pet is now a standard condition of every domestic violence protection order because lawmakers recognised exactly how offenders exploit the bond between victims and their animals. More than 40 US states have also strengthened protection orders to include companion animals.
"New Zealand is behind the curve. It's time our laws caught up with the reality of family violence.
"We know pets are often part of the family, and we know abusers deliberately target them. Victims stay longer in dangerous situations because they’re terrified of what will happen if they leave.

“Knowing all of that, doing nothing is not an option. ACT will put victims first, gives Police better tools, strengthen Protection Orders, and make it easier for victims to leave violence without leaving part of their family behind.
“Family violence is about power and control, and ACT won’t let abusers keep using pets to trap their victims.”
####### Rural
## Paris Needs to Change

ACT is announcing a science-based climate policy that puts New Zealand's interests first. If the Paris Agreement cannot accommodate targets that reflect the real warming impact of New Zealand's emissions, then New Zealand should leave it.
ACT’s proposed NDC would:

- Recognise a split gas approach that treats long-life gases like carbon dioxide and short-lived gases like methane differently. That is critical for recognising the efficiency of our agricultural sector.

- Revisit the Emissions Reduction Plans. ACT will reset these around realistic targets, the split-gas approach, and genuine environmental outcomes rather than compliance with a framework designed for industrialised economies with fundamentally different emissions profiles to ours.

- Keep agriculture out of the Emissions Trading Scheme. New Zealand dairy has a carbon footprint 46% lower than the global average. ACT opposes methane pricing because taxing the world's most emissions-efficient farmers won't change the climate. Putting a price on that isn't climate policy – it's a tax on the world's most efficient food producers, which makes your groceries more expensive while shifting production to countries that do it worse.
#### In our team’s words:

“New Zealand's farmers are the most emissions-efficient in the world, yet they are treated like climate villains and punished by climate targets that ignore the difference between methane from livestock and carbon from fossil fuels,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“The Paris Agreement provides a pathway for New Zealand to issue its own Nationally Determined Contribution. ACT is campaigning to do that in the next term of Parliament so we can have a plan that is ambitious for New Zealand and reflects the science of climate change.

“Under the current approach, prime farmland gets converted to pine trees, farmers face new costs for emissions they're already managing efficiently, and global emissions don't drop – because other countries with higher-footprint production simply fill the gap. That's not an environmental outcome. That's an economic and environmental own-goal.

"Current climate targets treat methane from a cow the same as carbon from a coal burner. That just isn’t scientific. “The result is that New Zealand farmers are being told to cut production while other countries increase output. That's not reducing global emissions, it's sending our jobs, our land, and our food production offshore – to countries that produce it less efficiently and with a higher carbon cost. It's exporting jobs, investment, and food production overseas.”

ACT Climate spokesperson Simon Court says: “ACT will submit a new Split-Gas emissions target that focuses on actual warming. Long-lived gases will continue on a path to lowering emissions, while biogenic methane will be managed under a No Additional Warming approach.

“We will also permanently keep agriculture out of the Emissions Trading Scheme. Taxing the world's most emissions-efficient farmers won't change the climate. It will just make food more expensive and push production into less efficient countries.
“ Last year, ACT made it clear that the Paris Agreement is broken and that New Zealand deserves a better climate deal. Today, we are putting forward exactly what that better deal looks like.

“New Zealand produces dairy with a carbon footprint 46% lower than the global average. We should be expanding our production, not retreating. ACT is the only party with the courage to stand up to the UN, rewrite the rules, and secure a future where farming grows.”
####### Hunters and Firearms
## Protect Lawful Hunting

Hunters acting safely and within the law can be deliberately obstructed by people who step into the line of fire to stop a shot. That creates an obvious danger, but there is no specific infringement offence for it.
Aircraft can also be used to harass game-bird shooters by deliberately scattering or flushing birds. This disturbs the birds and sabotages a lawful activity, with little legal remedy available.
People remain free to oppose hunting. They should not be free to interfere in ways that put others at risk.
Read the full policy here.
#### ACT will:
- Create an infringement offence for deliberately standing in the line of fire of a lawful hunter.
- Create an infringement offence for using drones or helicopters to harass game-bird shooters.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“A hunter acting safely and lawfully should not have someone step into the line of fire to stop a shot. That is not ordinary protest. It creates an immediate risk for everyone there, yet the law has no specific answer.

“Hunters and game-bird shooters are expected to follow strict safety rules, as they should. Those rules cannot work if someone deliberately enters the line of fire. The law needs a clear consequence for that behaviour.”
ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:
“The same principle applies when activists use drones or helicopters to scatter game birds. It disturbs the birds, disrupts a lawful shoot and can create another hazard in the air and on the ground.

“We would create a specific infringement offence for harassing game-bird shooters with an aircraft. If someone wants to campaign against hunting, they remain free to do so. They should not be free to sabotage a lawful activity in a way that puts people at risk.”
####### Law & Order
## Keeping Public Spaces Safe
New Zealanders deserve to feel safe at their local shops and transport hubs, and businesses deserve real tools to stand up for themselves and their communities.

Business owners want protection from trained, uniformed professionals. But Police can’t respond quickly to every call. Security professionals have the potential to fill the gap. New Zealand has twice as many licenced security officers as police officers, but they currently have no more authority than any other citizen.

ACT will give real power – with clear limits – to properly trained security professionals. We’ll introduce a new licence that security professionals can obtain, with training, to gain the authority needed to keep shared spaces and businesses safe.

The Government has already given some guards elevated powers with ad hoc legislation, such as Parliamentary Security. ACT will allow retailers, business associations, shopping strips, and transport operators to access a higher calibre of protection.
Under ACT's plan, licenced Accredited Security Operators would be able to:
- Require a person's name and address on private premises and detain them until Police arrive if they refuse and won't leave.
- Issue conduct-based exclusion notices, enforceable for up to three years across multiple premises – like those of a business association – held on a register under the Privacy Act.
- Remove people who threaten safety, cause damage, or breach a venue's conditions of entry.
- ⁠Use reasonable and proportionate force as a last resort, ceasing the moment the person complies or Police arrive.
- Carry out consent-based safety searches, including on the premises, where refusing a search means no entry.
Read the full policy
#### In our team’s words:

"Every licence holder will have to go through specialised advanced training and education. This is not something that any Tom, Dick, or Harry could just pick up. Stringent vetting will ensure only the right people with the right capability will be approved,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

"These powers will apply on private premises, but when combined with citizens’ arrest powers currently going through Parliament, will give licenced professionals real capability to keep the wider community safe.
"ACT’s policy will unlock communities’ potential to protect themselves, without relying solely on the taxpayer or a stretched Police force.”
ACT’s spokesperson for retail crime, Dr Parmjeet Parmar, says:
“Retail crime is still hurting businesses. When people don’t feel safe visiting their local shops, they stay home and shop online. That drains foot traffic and jobs out of town centres.

“Retail NZ’s Crime Report estimates that crime costs the sector $2.6 billion a year. Behind that number are shop owners and workers who have been threatened or harmed, and communities that feel unsafe.

“ACT’s policy means businesses can take real action, sharing the services of highly-effective security professionals. It reflects the reality that, until the Police arrive, communities need real authority to stand up for themselves against thieves and thugs."
####### Hunters and Firearms
## Hunter-Led Game Management

Game animals on conservation land are managed by DOC, an agency whose legislation still starts from controlling or exterminating them. The Game Animal Council was meant to give hunters a meaningful role, but it can advise while DOC keeps the authority.
That model treats hunters as another group to consult instead of trusting the people who understand the herds and spend time in the country where they live.

ACT would put responsibility in the hands of the Game Animal Council. Game animals would be managed sustainably within conservation limits, with proper recognition for the value that healthy herds bring to hunters and regional communities.
#### ACT will:
- Transfer responsibility for managing game animals on conservation land from DOC to the Game Animal Council.
- Fully fund the Council to carry out its current and proposed responsibilities.
- Recognise game-animal and game-bird species in relevant legislation as valued natural resources to be sustainably managed.
- Designate New Zealand’s most valued game herds as Herds of Special Interest, beginning with Stewart Island whitetail deer.
Read the full policy
#### In our team's words:
ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“Hunters have spent generations in the backcountry. They know the animals and the country because they are there every weekend, but Wellington still asks for their views after the real decisions have been made. Hunters should be helping to make those decisions from the start.

“The Game Animal Council was supposed to give hunters a genuine say. Instead, it was left advising DOC while DOC kept control. ACT would transfer game-animal management on conservation land to the Council and fund it properly to do the job.

“The law still begins from the idea that introduced game animals should be exterminated wherever possible. That makes no sense for valued herds that can be sustainably managed. ACT would recognise game animals and game birds as natural resources and use Herds of Special Interest to protect the best herds, starting with Stewart Island whitetail.”
ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“Healthy herds need proper targets and the surrounding environment needs protection. Hunters understand both sides of that equation. DOC would keep its wider conservation role, but the people who know the resource would make the game-management decisions.

“Hunters were promised a seat at the table and got another advisory role. They have earned real responsibility. The Game Animal Council should be judged on the results it delivers, not kept at arm’s length by the bureaucracy.”
####### Education
####### Economy & Cost of Living
## Affordable School Uniforms
A school uniform should identify a school, not lock families into buying every basic item from one supplier.

Many families spend well over $1,000 per child once they buy several shirts, socks, shorts or skirts, PE gear and replacements. In 2025, 38,000 WINZ hardship loans worth $11 million were issued to help families meet the cost.

Some state schools require everyday items to be bought from one approved supplier, even when an equivalent item is available at an ordinary retailer for much less. There is no educational reason for a logo to make a pair of navy socks cost several times more.
#### ACT will:
- Amend the Education and Training Act to limit state schools to a maximum of three compulsory branded uniform items.
- Require schools to offer generic alternatives for high-use items such as shorts, pants, skirts, skorts and socks.
- Let families buy those generic items from standard clothing retailers.
- Keep room for schools to choose a small number of branded items that preserve their identity and traditions.
- Exclude sports uniforms, team strips, kapa haka uniforms and tracksuits from the new rules.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Education spokesperson Laura McClure says:

“Many families are spending well over $1,000 per child once they buy several shirts, socks, shorts or skirts, PE gear, and replacements. Last year the Government issued 38,000 WINZ hardship loans worth $11 million for school uniforms. Parents should not have to go into debt for clothing that costs far more than it needs to.

“There is no educational reason for a pair of navy socks to cost three times as much because it has to come from one supplier. More competition and choice could put hundreds of dollars back in parents’ pockets without changing what children wear to school.”

####### Rural
## Let the Kid on the Bus
School transport rules are built around a child's nearest school. In rural communities, that can leave an empty seat passing a waiting child because their family chose a different school.
Parents then make the same trip in their own car or ute, spending time and fuel while a taxpayer-funded bus travels the route with room to spare.

ACT's Open Seat Rule would use that spare capacity. In most cases it would not require any extra spending. If demand fills a route, more buses could be funded from within the Ministry of Education's existing budget.
#### ACT will:
- Introduce an Open Seat Rule for school transport.
- Let any child living along an existing school bus route use the service when a seat is available, regardless of which school they attend.
- Provide an additional bus where demand on a route grows beyond its capacity.
- Fund any additional buses from within the Ministry of Education's existing budget by cutting waste.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT MP Andrew Hoggard says:

“In most cases this would not require any extra spending. If a route filled up, we would add buses and fund them from within the Ministry of Education’s existing budget by cutting waste. Money should get children to school, not be tied up in Wellington bureaucracy.

“The nearest-school rule does not reflect how rural communities live. Families choose schools based on where siblings go, the support available, and what works around jobs and farm life. They need flexibility, not hard-and-fast rules that leave children waiting and families paying for a second transport system.”
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“If a taxpayer-funded bus is already running with an empty seat, no child should be left on the roadside because of a Wellington rulebook. It is a small, common-sense change that saves families time and fuel while using the transport taxpayers have already paid for.”
####### Hunters and Firearms
## Back the Volunteers
DOC is responsible for more than 950 huts and 15,000 kilometres of tracks. It faces a 30 per cent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021.

Hunting, tramping and conservation groups already restore huts, maintain tracks and run trap lines at a fraction of the cost. Too often they survive on annual discretionary grants, with no certainty that they can keep the work going.
ACT would fund capable community groups to deliver the work and let accredited hunting groups earn nature credits for conservation results that can be independently verified
Read the full policy
#### ACT will:
- Require DOC to give community groups the first opportunity for funding when they can offer a competitive option for backcountry upkeep.
- Allow multi-year contracts so volunteer organisations can plan ahead instead of applying for funding year by year.
- Open the Voluntary Nature Credits Market to accredited hunting groups so they can earn credits for verified biodiversity results.
- Require formal representation for the New Zealand Deerstalkers Association and Game Animal Council in predator-removal decisions affecting hunters.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“DOC has more than 950 huts and 15,000 kilometres of tracks to look after. It faces a 30 per cent maintenance shortfall and has issued more than 2,300 closure alerts since 2021. The department will not clear that backlog on its own.

“Community groups already restore huts and maintain tracks at a fraction of the cost, but many survive from one discretionary grant to the next. ACT would give them the first opportunity for funding when they can offer a competitive option, including the security of multi-year contracts.”
ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“Hunters are already in the hills running trap lines and removing predators, but the new nature-credit market does not recognise that work. Accredited hunting groups should be able to earn credits when they can show they have delivered real biodiversity gains.

“The New Zealand Deerstalkers Association and Game Animal Council should be formally represented when predator-removal operations affecting hunters are planned. Decisions are better when the people already doing the work are involved from the start, not consulted after everything has been settled.”
ACT candidate and former New Zealand Deerstalkers Association president Callum Sheridan says:

“The hunting community contributes hundreds of thousands of unpaid hours to conservation every year. Backing those groups to deliver measurable results would mean more work gets done in the backcountry and taxpayers get better value for their money.”
####### Economy & Cost of Living
####### Infrastructure
## Local Tourism Dividend

Tourism supports businesses and jobs throughout New Zealand, but the communities that host visitors also carry the costs. Visitor numbers put pressure on local roads, wastewater systems, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, public spaces and other council infrastructure.

Visitors pay GST, and international visitors also pay the International Visitor Levy. Central government collects that revenue, while councils and their ratepayers meet many of the local costs. ACT’s Local Tourism Dividend will return $1 to a community for every commercial guest night it hosts.

The more visitors a community attracts, the more support it will receive. This applies the same principle ACT has secured for housing growth: when councils help enable economic activity that generates revenue for central government, they should share in the benefits.
ACT's full Local Tourism Dividend policy can be found here.
#### ACT will:
- Make an automatic annual payment to every territorial authority of $1 for each domestic and international commercial guest night recorded in its area through the Accommodation Data Programme.
- Base each payment on the most recently completed 12 months of guest-night data.
- Require no applications, matching funding or negotiations with central government.
- Provide approximately $40.6 million a year to councils based on 2026 guest nights, including $8.2 million for Auckland, $4.9 million for Queenstown and $2 million for Rotorua.

- Give councils flexibility to fund local roads, parking, water and wastewater infrastructure, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, public spaces, visitor amenities, events infrastructure and other services affected by visitor demand.
- Allow the Dividend to replace rates funding already being spent on eligible services, reducing the burden on local ratepayers.
- Fund the Dividend from the existing tourism appropriation instead of imposing a new bed tax that would raise prices and create more bureaucracy for accommodation businesses.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:
“Councils will receive $1 for every guest night in their area, funded from the GST and visitor levies tourists already pay.

“If revenues allow and councils use funds wisely, the $1 rate may rise over time. This policy fixes a real problem without adding another charge to the hotel bill or expanding government,” says Mr Seymour.
“Households and businesses live within their means. Government should too. New taxes start small and tend to grow - this policy avoids that trap and keeps prices competitive for visitors.

“New Zealand is a top tourist destination but that success causes strains on local infrastructure. Ratepayers are too often left to pick up the bill. ACT’s Local Tourism Dividend gives councils the funding to keep pace, easing pressure on wastewater, public toilets, rubbish collection, freedom-camping facilities, and other services.

## ACT sets the No New Taxes agenda
#### “ACT is chalking up a taxpayer victory, after the National Party has adopted a version of our local tourism dividend," says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour
“ACT is chalking up a taxpayer victory, after the National Party has adopted a version of our local tourism dividend," says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“About two weeks after ACT pledged No New Taxes, the National Party followed suit. A few days later we announced a Local Tourism Dividend policy as an alternative to a Bed Tax, National has adopted a version of that policy as well.
"ACT is proud to have shaped the debate on this issue, when so many parties wanted to introduce a new tax, there is now a clear pathway to solve the same problem without a new tax.
“This is good news for the next Government, should we be re-elected. It is also another example of the value of ACT. We hold the line against new taxes, then come up with a better solution.

“As I said while announcing the policy, if revenues allow and councils use funds wisely, the $1 rate may rise over time. This policy fixes a real problem without adding another charge to the hotel bill or expanding government.

“It is a smarter alternative to a bed tax because it doesn’t impose a compliance burden on businesses, there is no new charge on the hotel bill, no new tax administration, and no legislation required to establish another tax. It uses the existing $185 billion revenue of the Government and Councils, rather than making the Government bigger.
"If there is a cut-and-dried case of the difference the ACT Party makes, it is the absence of a bed tax, a bank tax and the stamp duty on houses National would have put in place given the chance.
“Without ACT around the Cabinet table holding firm on No New Taxes, New Zealanders would already be paying more.

"ACT Ministers have driven $14 billion of savings across three Budgets, helping avoid more debt, taxes, and pressure on interest rates. That discipline has helped put the Government on a path back to surplus a year earlier, but it needs to be delivered year on year.

"A party vote for ACT is a steadfast anchor against the pressure for higher taxes and bigger government. This won’t be the last time the fiscal pressure comes on and our friends are tempted to eat the tax apple from the wrong tree. To balance the books with No New Taxes, Party Vote ACT in 2026."

“ACT will bring balance to New Zealand’s immigration system by introducing physical presence requirements for permanent residents, ensuring visa holders have a genuine commitment to our country,” says ACT’s Immigration spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar. “The strangest immigration policy we have is that permanent residents don’t have to be permanently resident. "New Zealand is, and should be, a welcoming country for migrants, but the privileges of permanent residence must reflect a real and lasting connection to our nation. “ACT is proposing to change New Zealand’s residence system. Under our policy, the existing Permanent Resident Visa category will be removed, and the existing Resident Visa changed to require all Resident Visa holders to receive a 5 year travel facility, replacing the current 2 year initial travel condition. “To maintain the travel facility, visa holders would need to be physically present in New Zealand for at least 730 days (2 years) within any rolling five-year period. The 730 days would not need to be continuous, but the indefinite, unconditional right to leave and re-enter the country would be removed. This ensures that those who want the ability to travel to New Zealand as residents must continue to demonstrate a meaningful connection with our country. “There will be exemptions for individuals working overseas for New Zealand employers, accompanying family members, military personnel serving overseas, and those with a citizen spouse, or other compelling humanitarian reasons. "This would also create a clearer answer to the question, what is the difference between permanent residence and citizenship? Right now, the two have nearly identical everyday rights. By introducing standard travel conditions, we create an evident distinction, giving people a reason to graduate to citizenship. "This change ensures that permanent residence reflects a genuine, ongoing commitment to New Zealand. “To unlock New Zealand’s potential, there needs to be a balance between rights and responsibilities. ## ACT to campaign on making Student Services Fees voluntary
#### ACT will campaign to make Student Services Fees voluntary – a move that would offer students real cost relief and ensure they are not forced to fund union activity.
Parmjeet Parmar
ACT will campaign to make Student Services Fees voluntary – a move that would offer students real cost relief and ensure they are not forced to fund union activity.

“Every domestic university student currently pays a compulsory Student Services Fee of up to $1,253 a year on top of tuition. Across a three-year degree this can add more than $4,000 to a student’s loan*. Because student loans are subsidised by the taxpayer, the compulsory fee also costs the taxpayer," says ACT Tertiary Education spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar.

“In 2011 ACT passed Voluntary Student Membership. As a result, students are no longer forced to join a student union. But universities have undermined the spirit of Voluntary Student Membership by absorbing the old association fee into a compulsory levy that students still cannot refuse. So, true freedom of association remains unfinished business.

“ACT will amend the regulations so universities must offer student services as a menu. Students would select the services they want and pay only for those, from fitness facilities to students unions and student media. Services not chosen would still be available on a transparent user-pays basis.
“Students should not be forced to fund unions, advocacy or student media they do not support. That is a matter of principle for ACT.

“Right now, student unions are running political campaigns to influence the election. They might even campaign to stop this policy. Students are forced to fund this activism, even if they disagree with it. ACT says unions are free to campaign, but no-one should be forced to fund them.

“Voluntary fees mean better-run services. If a union or any other university service struggles to attract willing subscribers, it can do what any other organisation or business does – improve its offering, or scale back its spending.

“ACT's policy will also restore the independence of unions to challenge university leadership. Unions are meant to hold the bosses to account, but there's a huge conflict of interest when they're dependent on the university for funding.

“Our policy would let students save up to around $4,000 on their student loan over the course of a degree. It would also save the taxpayer money, because student debt is subsidised. We will complete the unfinished business of Voluntary Student Membership and restore genuine choice.”
Editor's note:
*After annual increases to the fee.

## One Law for All, One Future Together
#### ACT has refined its plans to tackle the high church of Treatyism in its next term of Government.
Free Press
#### The Haps

Parliament was in recess last week, but politics continued. ACT celebrated David Seymour’s reforms to school attendance with record numbers (11,579) of Not Enrolled students returned to school in the first half of this year. Charter school enrolments, meanwhile, increased 18 per cent in six months. Many charter schools are now looking for bigger buildings because space is their constraint. Giving communities a chance to compete for education funding is ACT philosophy in action, and it’s transforming lives let down by the state system.

The Party also released new policy that was welcomed as ‘a breath of fresh air and common sense.’ The Local Tourism Dividend would give a Council one dollar for each bed night tourists stay in the Council’s area.

It would help Councils support tourism without a new tax to administer. Councils and tourism operators have been braying for a new tax for years, ACT strongly opposes any new tax, because once they’re in, they always grow. The policy, and five reasons why it’s better than a new tax, are here.
#### One Law for All, One Future Together
The current Government was elected to fix the rampant and deliberate racism that grew up under its predecessor.

Since November 2023 it has: removed the separatist Māori Health Authority, given communities a referendum on Māori words, cancelled Three Waters with its co-governed boards, replaced the ‘Aotearoa Histories Curriculum’ with a balanced view of human history in New Zealand, issued a Cabinet Circular that services must be delivered on need, not race, so things like diabetes medicines and bowel cancer screening are no longer funded along racial lines… We could go on, but the point is a lot has been done.

For all the progress that has been made, though, there is a niggling feeling that the public service has carried on its merry way, giving a big fat finger to the Government of the day. It shows up when karakia are required at the start of meetings, job ads advertise for knowledge of te ao Māori (but no other culture), and people lose out because they didn’t ‘demonstrate their commitment to te tiriti in the home.’

Last week’s Free Press argued that Treatyism has become New Zealand’s new religion. Colonisation was the original sin, but if you wear the adornments around your neck, practice the rituals before your meetings, and smite non-believers as ‘racist’ then, maybe, you will be saved.

The Public Service has become the church of New Zealand’s new religion, and if you doubt that you only need to look at the Ministry of Education’s Tātai Pou Competency Matrix. A workers’ competency is ranked from ‘unsatisfactory’ to ‘high.’ You don’t just need to promote Treatyism to move up the matrix, you need to promote it to others to be highly competent.
If you are not a believer, even not practicing in your home, you may not get a job in the public service.

Missionaries would be proud, but our country was built on secularism and tolerance. The Treaty says every New Zealander should have the ‘same rights and duties’. In 1847, between the Treaty and the first Parliament, Governor Grey issued an education ordinance requiring school instruction to be secular for parents who demanded it, while acknowledging many parents would want religious instruction. Parliament’s 1877 Education Act also demanded education be secular.

Not long after that, Kate Sheppard, perhaps the greatest New Zealander and a devout Christian, said “All that separates, whether it be of race, class, creed or sex, is inhuman and must be overcome.” A century later New Zealanders protested en masse against apartheid, even at the expense of seeing the ABs.

New Zealand is a society founded, at least in part, on secularism and racial equality. What is happening in the Public Service, in spite of the elected Government, is counter to the foundations of secular tolerance this country is built on, and must be overcome.

That’s why the ACT Party has launched policy to remove Section 73 of the Public Service Act 2020, the section that requires the Public Service carry out discriminatory hiring. The Party pledges to upgrade its successful Need-not-Race Cabinet Circular to law enforceable in Court. It will ban taxpayer financing for cultural practices. It pledges to separate spiritual rituals from government work.

The full policy is here, but one question remains. Wasn’t this done already? Yes, ACT negotiated to reform the Public Service Act, and improvements were made. The roughest edges of that law made under the Labour-Green-New Zealand First Government in 2020 have been knocked off. The new Section 11A says Chief Executives should focus on performance first.

But, even Free Press underestimated the religious fervour that drives Treatyism. Learning from this term of Government, ACT has refined its plans to tackle the high church of Treatyism in its next term of Government.
#### A way to help
If you like what ACT has been saying and doing, and want to see us return after the election with an even stronger team, here’s a good way to help.
Friends of ACT, Grace and Jonathan Ayling, have generously donated a special run of ACT Pinot Noir, with all profits going directly towards ACT’s 2026 election campaign.

Sunday, 28 June 2026
## ACT unveils plan for radically simpler, smaller government

#### “New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand’s potential,” says ACT Leader Seymour.
David Seymour
“Making New Zealand affordable again must start at the top," says ACT Leader Seymour, announcing ACT's plan for a simpler, smaller government at the Party's 2026 Rally.
“New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand’s potential," says Mr Seymour.
“Today ACT is setting out the next level of detail in our policy with fewer departments, fewer ministers, and clear lines of accountability so taxpayers pay less and get better services.

“New Zealand has 78 ministerial portfolios, 28 ministers, and 43 departments. Norway has a similar population and runs with 20 ministers across 17 ministries. New Zealand’s oversized Government isn’t intentional, it’s like a hedge that stopped being trimmed years ago.

“The result is a Government that is too tangled to act. Housing, infrastructure, welfare dependency, crime, and health all cut across multiple agencies. When seven departments share a problem, it can stop being anyone’s job to solve it. Kiwis are left frustrated, bouncing between departments or denied straight answers.

“Sprawling, tangled bureaucracy is expensive. It costs money that can’t be returned to taxpayers, can’t pay down debt, can’t reach the nurse, teacher or police officer on the frontline, and can’t build the infrastructure we need.”
Under ACT’s plan:
• The 43 departments would be consolidated into 19 coherent departments.
• The 78 overlapping portfolios with 28 ministers would be collapsed into just 18 ministers.
• Each department would report to one minister for its budget and outcomes.*
• Ministers would be allowed to appoint chief executives for a fixed term, renewable once, with clear protections for officials.

• Chief executives could be removed by Ministers for specified reasons such as non-performance or policy misalignment, but they would retain public service protections and the right to return to a lower classified role.
• Operational independence would be protected by law for agencies that need it, such as Police, NZSIS, and NZDF.
ACT’s full proposal, ' ACT’s plan for a consolidated bureaucracy', can be found here.

“Overseas research shows more ministers with spending power means bigger deficits. When many ministers each control part of the budget, but the cost falls on the whole tax base, each has an incentive to grow their own spending while bearing only a fraction of the cost.
“ACT’s plan won’t affect frontline services like nurses, teachers, or police. If anything, it will make them more effective with clear lines of responsibility and a focus on their core role.

“The Coalition Government has accepted the argument for a smaller Government, but current changes are tinkering around the edges. Kiwis are tired of piecemeal change that takes forever, so ACT is proposing a thought-out plan for the whole government, that we can start rolling out immediately in the next term.

“ACT would also fix the broken accountability line between ministers and departmental chief executives. At the moment, ministers are held responsible for delivery, but they do not appoint the person leading the department responsible for that delivery. ACT would remove the Public Service Commission and allow ministers to appoint chief executives, and chief executives could be removed for specified reasons.

“That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential. A government with clear structure and limits, not the tangled result of accidental growth. Small enough to be accountable, simple enough to act, and focused on results for New Zealanders instead of managing itself.”
*Except for the newly-created MCERT.

## ACT announces policy to make benefits a hand-up, not a way of life
#### ACT Leader David Seymour today announced new welfare policy to restore fairness, personal responsibility, and the value of work to New Zealand’s benefit system
David Seymour
ACT today announced new welfare policy to restore fairness, personal responsibility, and the value of work to New Zealand’s benefit system.
“Welfare should unlock potential, not trap it. So why are we paying people to stay at home who could be doing jobs we are currently filling with migrants?" says ACT Leader Seymour.

“New Zealanders believe in helping people through tough times. But the deal has to be fair: if you can work, you should be taking real steps toward work, and taxpayer support should go to the essentials it was intended to fund.

“Under Labour, benefit dependency became normalised. The number of people on Jobseeker benefits has increased 73% in the past ten years. Jobseeker benefits alone now cost more than we spending on policing, and twice as much as the medicines budget.

“Behind those numbers are real people whose potential is being wasted. Every person who could work but is left on welfare is a life held back, a family with fewer opportunities, and a country that is poorer than it needs to be.”
ACT’s policy has two planks:
##### Tightening medical certification for health-related benefits

- All health and disability benefits will be independently issued by an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors.* A person’s usual GP or specialist will still be able to provide medical history, clinical notes, and supporting evidence.
- Assessments will be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion.
- Existing Jobseeker Support – Health Condition or Disability and Supported Living Payment recipients will be reassessed against the new criteria on a phased basis.
- Reassessment will begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic, where much of the recent growth has occurred.
- ACT will allow for long-term arrangements for those with a genuine, enduring disability or health condition so support stays in place for those who truly need it.
*The Government has already established this as an option, but ACT will make it mandatory.
##### Managed assistance for long-term Jobseeker recipients
- ACT will introduce electronic money management for Jobseeker Support Work Ready recipients who remain on a benefit for more than four months.*
- Their benefit will be delivered through an electronic payment card directed to essentials such as groceries, rent, power, transport, health and childcare.
- The card will block spending on alcohol, gambling, tobacco, and cash withdrawals.
- ACT will include carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.
*New Zealand already has money management as an option in certain circumstances, but ACT will make it mandatory after the four-month threshold.

“Health-related welfare is one of the fastest-growing pressure points in the system. ⁠In ten years the number of New Zealanders on a health or disability Jobseeker benefit has nearly doubled, to 96,852. Another 96,000 are on the Supported Living Payment. Most of the growth is from new claims for psychological or psychiatric conditions
“Supported Living Payment recipients remain on benefit for an average of 13.3 years, while Jobseeker Health Condition or Disability recipients remain on benefit for an average of 6.1 years.

“Nobody should be denied support when they genuinely cannot work. But the public deserves confidence that the system is not being gamed, and that people are not being written off when work or greater independence is possible.

“Electronic money management means taxpayer support will not fund purchases that make it harder for people to get their lives back on track. If someone is receiving a benefit funded by working New Zealanders, that support should go to food, housing, power, transport, health, and childcare – not alcohol, gambling, or tobacco.

“Unlocking New Zealand’s potential means unlocking the potential of New Zealanders. That starts with a welfare system that backs people to move forward, rewards effort, protects taxpayers, and refuses to write people off."

## ACT will introduce smarter screening to improve child safety

#### ACT will campaign on introducing the Working with Children Card, a streamlined system for ensuring that any person who works with children has been properly vetted and is checked continuously for safety, says ACT’s Children spokesperson Karen Chhour.
Karen Chhour

ACT will campaign on introducing the Working with Children Card, a streamlined system for ensuring that any person who works with children has been properly vetted and is checked continuously for safety, says ACT’s Children spokesperson Karen Chhour.
“Parents should be able to leave their children with a teacher, coach, afterschool carer, or volunteer knowing the adults around them are safe to work with children.

“The current system does not provide that reassurance. Safety checks are carried out by individual employers and generally only re-checked every three years. This provides only a snapshot of a person at one point in time, with no consistent system for identifying risks that emerge between checks.

“The Working with Children Card would give parents confidence that their children are in safe hands. It follows the worker, is continuously monitored, considers additional relevant information, and replaces duplicated screening by individual organisations.
“Eligibility for the card will take into account relevant criminal convictions, disciplinary findings, and other records relating to children or child-related work.

“People who work with children have to undergo the same checks every time they start or change jobs. ACT’s plan would cut out the duplication and bureaucracy. Once issued, the card could be used across eligible jobs, schools, clubs, businesses, and community organisations. Employers would simply verify that the person holds a valid card.

“Placing the ownership with the individual rather than the employer will free up police and Ministry of Justice resources, and make it easier for small organisations to meet their child-safety responsibilities.
“The system ensures that cardholders are safe the whole time they work with children, not just up until a check was last completed.

“ACT will link the Working with Children Card to ongoing information from Police and relevant regulatory bodies, keeping it continuously up to date. If a cardholder is charged with a disqualifying offence, their card could be suspended or revoked and their employer notified. Employers would no longer have to wait for the next three-year check to discover that a worker’s circumstances have changed.

"It can take three years for a person's offending to be reported to their employer. In Queensland they update continuously with a similar system called the Blue Card. Last year they cancelled 2,438 people's Blue Cards due to up-to-the-minute information. In New Zealand those people would still be working with children.
“The Working with Children Card gives parents peace of mind about their child’s safety, and creates a smarter, less burdensome screening process for employers and workers.”

## ACT unveils plan for New Zealand’s first dedicated Cancer centre - Beyond Tomorrow

#### “ACT will build New Zealand’s Starship for Cancer, the country’s first purpose-built comprehensive cancer centre, with two campuses in Auckland and Christchurch,” says ACT List Candidate Paul Henry.
Paul Henry
“ACT will build New Zealand’s Starship for Cancer, the country’s first purpose-built comprehensive cancer centre, with two campuses in Auckland and Christchurch,” says ACT List Candidate Paul Henry.
“Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year, by 2044 that number is expected to exceed 45,000.
“I’ve joined politics because I am ambitious for New Zealand and think it has endless potential. We should not accept being second-rate at treating a disease that touches almost every family.
“Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer.

“This is an aspirational policy, but it is realistic and practical. Comprehensive cancer centres are the gold standard internationally because they bring researchers, clinicians, universities, private providers and philanthropists together with world-class treatment, technology and clinical trials. They also help attract and retain the best oncologists, surgeons and scientists. If New Zealand cannot offer that environment, Australia and other countries will.

“The centres will be developed using a combination of public-private partnership financing, charitable donations, existing Crown health investment, and other private capital where appropriate. The indicative capital requirement is around $2 billion, with the final cost determined through the detailed business-case process.
“By partnering with New Zealand’s leading philanthropists, families, businesses, charitable trusts, community organisations and successful Kiwis, we can build something extraordinary.

“ACT will establish an independent philanthropic foundation from the beginning of the project to unlock extraordinary generosity, with major donors recognised through naming rights for appropriate parts of the Centres, including, for a transformational contribution, potentially a hospital itself.

“The recently introduced $33,333 cap on the tax benefits available for charitable donations will be removed for all charitable giving. If New Zealanders want to give $1 million, $10 million or more to cancer care, medical research or other causes, the tax system should encourage that generosity, not impose an arbitrary ceiling on it.

“This is an investment in New Zealand’s future. It is the type of project that makes New Zealand the envy of the world and attracts private healthcare investment, new technologies and therapies, teaching, medical research, and international clinical trials.
“New Zealand can build one of the world’s great cancer institutions. ACT will make it happen.”

## ACT will stop any proposed VPN ban
#### "ACT will prevent any ban on VPNs," says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour
"ACT will prevent any ban on VPNs," says ACT Leader David Seymour.
"The Government is united in condemning China’s missile launch, and to be consistent it’s critical we don’t adopt Chinese-style intrusions into internet privacy.
" Speculation over a VPN ban exposes the problem with well-intentioned efforts to protect children from harm.

“Any ban strong enough to stop a motivated teenager is strong enough to violate all of our privacy. On the other hand, motivated teenagers will skirt anything weaker in an instant. The Australians have found this, with 80 per cent of teens ignoring the ban.

"If a teenager can bypass a social media ban with a VPN, then the ban isn't effective. If the Government responds by restricting VPNs, it is no longer regulating children's access to social media, it is regulating how every New Zealander uses the internet.

"VPNs are legitimate privacy and security tools. Businesses use them to protect commercial information. Journalists use them to protect sources. Ordinary New Zealanders use them to secure their personal information on public Wi-Fi. They are an essential part of modern cybersecurity.

"ACT was very clear on this point when we filed our differing view on the social media inquiry: 'The countries that have placed restrictions on VPNs include North Korea, China, Russia, Turkmenistan, and Iran. These countries use these restrictions to suppress their citizens' free speech, often in the name of protecting from online harm.'
"New Zealand should not be borrowing ideas from the authoritarian internet playbook. We should be defending the values that separate free countries from controlled ones.

"Social media harms for children are real, but any response must work for adults too. If making a ban work requires controlling the privacy tools used by ordinary people, then it's time admit the policy doesn't work and pursue better solutions."
####### Economy & Cost of Living
####### Infrastructure
## Innovation Trials
Technology changes faster than the rulebook. Agricultural drones, driverless cars and new medical treatments are already being used overseas. In New Zealand, old rules can keep them out for years.

An Innovation Trial would let the Government set aside a particular rule for a limited test in one place. The approval would state the safety conditions and how the result will be measured. Bad results end the trial. Good results give the Government evidence to change the rule.
Government sometimes makes these exceptions after a company finds the right officials and persuades them to act. ACT would publish one application process that any company could use.
#### ACT will:
- Publish a permanent application process for Innovation Trials.
- Allow a specific regulation to be set aside for a limited test in one location.
- Set safety conditions and a way to measure the result before a trial begins.
- Use the Ministry for Regulation to help agencies identify existing exemption powers and run trials consistently.
- Invite companies working on autonomous vehicles, agricultural drones and medical technology to run trials in New Zealand.
Read David Seymour's speech
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Technology is what ultimately drives wages. People in the United States, Japan, Britain and Europe are using inventions that remain illegal here. Every year we wait leaves New Zealand workers further behind.

“Take agricultural spray drones. Once a drone weighs more than 25 kilograms, certification can cost up to $2,000 and take over a year. Australian farmers can use drones weighing up to 150 kilograms under a simple licence. Our officials have put the issue on a two-year work programme.

“An Innovation Trial lets the Government set aside the relevant rule for a limited test. The trial has conditions and an end date. We collect the evidence, see what actually happens and decide whether the old rule still makes sense.

“ACT will make that process available to any company through a permanent public application. New Zealand can then go to the people developing driverless cars, medical treatments and new farm technology and say: bring it here and prove it works.”
####### Infrastructure
## A Fair Contribution for Infrastructure

New Zealand needs immigration. Employers cannot find every nurse, software engineer or farm worker they need within a working-age population of about three million. Migrants bring skills and help businesses grow.

Population growth also puts immediate pressure on housing and infrastructure. A temporary worker can use roads and public services from the day they arrive, before they have paid much New Zealand tax.

ACT will add a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas. It would sit on top of existing visa charges and is expected to raise about $80 million a year. At that rate, comparable visas would remain cheaper than those in Australia and the United Kingdom.
#### ACT will:
- Add a $6-a-day infrastructure surcharge to temporary work visas, on top of existing charges.
- Require temporary workers to contribute to New Zealand's infrastructure from their first day in the country.
Read ACT’s full immigration policy
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealand still needs immigration. No modern export economy with a working-age population of about three million can produce every nurse, software engineer and farm worker it needs. Our economy and public services depend on people bringing skills here.
“That support cannot be taken for granted. Immigration has to work for the people already here, and population growth cannot be allowed to run down the infrastructure earlier generations built.

“At $6 a day, the visa would remain more affordable than comparable visas in Australia and the United Kingdom. Asking temporary workers to help with infrastructure is a fair part of an immigration system that keeps public confidence.”
####### Law & Order
####### Immigration
## Deport Serious Offenders
Immigration must work for New Zealand. The system should welcome people, but only if they share values of tolerance, freedom and democracy, help build infrastructure, and play by the rules.
Today, Kiwis who are proud of our settler heritage are asking themselves why something doesn’t quite feel right with immigration. ACT believes their suspicions are correct.

Successive governments have let a skilled-migration system become a general-purpose labour tap. They have failed to enforce the rules they set. They have allowed infrastructure to fall further behind. And they have asked too little of people who want to benefit from the Kiwi character without supporting it.
ACT’s policy restores the basic bargain that New Zealand was built on. People are welcome here if they contribute, respect our democratic values, and help build the country.
ACT’s six-point immigration plan is:
1.⁠ ⁠Deport serious offenders

ACT will ensure Resident Visa holders convicted of offences carrying sentences of 10 years or more can be deported no matter how long they’ve been here. This goes further than the Government’s current proposal to extend liability to 20 years.
2.⁠ ⁠Skilled visas for skilled jobs

Accredited Employer Work Visas are meant to fill crucial skills gaps, but too often the gaps close and the categories remain wide open. ACT will have each skill category automatically expire every year. To remain open, they would need to show up-to-date evidence of demand.
3.⁠ ⁠Opportunity, not dependency

ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for all residence class visa holders. That means no jobseeker support, accommodation supplement, or income-tested benefits for a migrant’s first five years here.
4.⁠ ⁠A fair contribution for infrastructure

ACT will introduce a $6 per day infrastructure surcharge on temporary work visas, on top of existing charges. This ensures migrants contribute to New Zealand’s infrastructure from day one, before they start paying tax. The fee is expected to raise around $80 million a year, while remaining more affordable than comparable visas in Australia and the United Kingdom.
5.⁠ ⁠Stronger English language requirements
ACT will extend basic English language requirements to all AEWV types. Lower standards will still be permitted for seasonal workers.
6.⁠ ⁠Enforce the rules

There are 20,980 known overstayers in New Zealand right now. ACT will establish a dedicated overstayer enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand. Platform employers such as Uber and DoorDash will be required to verify and report work rights. Employers who facilitate overstaying will lose their accreditation.
Read the full policy
#### In our team’s words:

“New Zealand is a settler society. From those who arrived in open boats 700 years ago, to those who arrived at Auckland Airport this morning, our country has been built by people willing to make a journey to try and build something better,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Immigration has enriched New Zealand. In less than 200 years, New Zealand has gone from a series of isolated villages, to a network of modern cities connected by road, rail, air, and sea, with electricity, the internet, and the three waters.

“Each wave of settlement has also built the Kiwi character that is respected around the world. Kiwis are recognised in everything from business to sport to peacekeeping as resourceful and thoughtful, firm but fair people who keep their word and can fix anything.
“We need an immigration system that recognises New Zealand’s heritage as a nation of settlers. We need new migrants to grow and develop, but that migration must work for New Zealand.
“Success requires a common set of expectations; respect our freedoms, uphold our democratic values, contribute to infrastructure, speak English, obey the law, and fill genuine gaps in the economy.”
