## Disrupt the Class, Leave the Class
Most students behave well and want to learn. Serious or persistent disruption can take over a lesson, leaving the teacher to manage one student while everyone else waits.

The Education Review Office found in 2024 that around half of teachers deal with disruption in every lesson. Forty-seven per cent lose 40 to 50 minutes or more each day responding to challenging behaviour. In the 2022 PISA results, New Zealand had the worst behavioural climate in maths classes in the OECD. Half of teachers told ERO that behaviour had a large impact on whether they intended to remain in teaching.

ACT would create a quick response that sits below formal stand-down and suspension processes. A teacher could direct a seriously or persistently disruptive student to leave and go to a staffed, supervised space. A refusal would be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refused again after that escalation, staff could use reasonable force to remove them.

Removed students would stay under supervision in a pastoral office, dean's room or learning support room. Empty or lockable rooms could not be used. Corporal punishment would remain illegal. Any physical intervention would have to be reasonable, proportionate and authorised by law.
Read ACT's full policy, Strengthening teacher authority and stopping class disruption, here.
#### ACT will:

- Amend the Education and Training Act 2020 to give classroom teachers an explicit legal power to direct a student to leave for serious or persistent disruption and report to a staffed, supervised space.
- Require a refusal to be escalated to a dean or senior leader. If the student refuses a second lawful direction after that escalation, staff may use reasonable force to remove them.
- Clarify section 99 of the Act so staff are protected when they use reasonable and proportionate intervention to prevent harm or the destruction of property.

- Require immediate removal followed by a mandatory stand-down or suspension for any assault on a teacher, student or other member of school staff. An assault that crosses the criminal threshold would be referred to Police Youth Aid on the first occurrence.

- Require a parent or guardian meeting when behaviour becomes serious or repeated, and when a student refuses a lawful direction to leave. Parents already working with the school in good faith over low-level disruption would not be called to a duplicate meeting.

- Escalate cases where a parent does not engage, either to the Ministry of Education or through the Oranga Tamariki and Police Youth Aid pathway. A parent who misses a mandatory meeting without a reasonable excuse could be fined up to $300 for a first offence and up to $3,000 for a later offence.
- Allow schools to recover the cost of deliberate property damage from a student's parents as a debt if it is not paid.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Candidate Paul Henry says:

“Education is the key to a better tomorrow. Somehow, we've allowed disruptive students to steal valuable learning time from their classmates while teachers are denied the authority to stop them. How can we expect teachers to administer world-class education if we are not providing them with world-class support?”

“Most students behave well and want to learn. They should not have their education held hostage by a minority who refuse to respect their teacher or classmates. We should be supporting teachers and education.

“Corporal punishment would remain illegal, and removed students would stay supervised. Any physical intervention must be reasonable, proportionate and backed by law. A teacher's job is to teach. ACT will give them the authority to get on with it.”

Tuesday, 8 September 2026
## Only ACT will cut the Carbon Tax
#### “Chris Hipkins wants to put the Carbon price up, National wants to keep it the same, only ACT is campaigning to bring it down and lower costs on New Zealanders,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour
“Chris Hipkins wants to put the Carbon price up, National wants to keep it the same, only ACT is campaigning to bring it down and lower costs on New Zealanders,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Less than two weeks after promising not to increase fuel taxes, Chris Hipkins is now complaining that the carbon price is too low. You can’t tell New Zealanders you’re worried about the price at the pump while campaigning to increase costs that flow through petrol, power, freight and groceries.

“Today’s carbon auction illustrates just how detached climate policy has become from economic reality. The Government refuses to sell carbon credits for less than $71, while exactly the same units have recently traded on the market for around $50.

“We would remove the artificial auction price floor so the Government can sell units at the price the market is actually willing to pay, and scrap wasteful bureaucracy such as the Climate Change Commission.
“And instead of treating carbon revenue as another pot of money for politicians to spend, we would return 100 per cent of the net revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund.
“At a carbon price of around $55, the ETS already costs an average household an estimated $478 a year. Labour now wants to increase that cost on Kiwis, while only ACT has a plan to reduce it.
“Sensible climate policy should preserve jobs and an affordable life while ensuring New Zealand does no more than the countries we trade and compete with.

“ACT would scrap the arbitrary Net Zero 2050 target and repeal the Zero Carbon Act. Instead of deliberately imposing costs our competitors are unwilling to bear, we would match them so New Zealand maintains market access without exporting Kiwi jobs.
“ACT will cut unnecessary costs, protect Kiwi jobs, return carbon revenue to households and let innovation deliver cleaner solutions.
“Cut the waste, grow the country, and unlock New Zealand’s potential.”

## Carbon auction farce why ACT will cut the Carbon Tax
#### “Barring a miracle, tomorrow’s carbon auction will further expose the absurdity of a climate policy that has lost touch with economic reality,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour
“Barring a miracle, tomorrow’s carbon auction will further expose the absurdity of a climate policy that has lost touch with economic reality,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“The Government will miss out on around $195 million dollars of revenue, under ACT’s policy that could be given to households as a Carbon Dividend. Instead, the price will stay artificially high and instead of getting a dividend, families will pay extra on their power and petrol.
“Sensible climate policy should preserve jobs and an affordable life while ensuring New Zealand does no more than the countries we trade and compete with.

“Every party except ACT supported the Zero Carbon Act. That led to crazy climate targets and settings that now mean the Government refuses to sell carbon credits for less than $71, when exactly the same units are trading on the market for around $50.
“No rational buyer is going to pay $71 for something they can buy for $50.

“In three years only two of 24 auctions have sold a unit. The last six Government auctions have failed to sell a single unit. Tomorrow, as a result, there will be up to 3.9 million units available. Unless something dramatically changes, taxpayers are staring at another auction where the Government prices itself out of its own market.
“It is a lose-lose. The Government gets no auction revenue and households and businesses still face the Carbon Tax through higher petrol, power, freight and grocery prices.
“ACT would cut the waste in climate policy so we can grow the country.

“We would scrap the arbitrary Net Zero 2050 target and repeal the Zero Carbon Act. Instead of imposing costs our competitors are unwilling to bear, we would match them so we maintain market access without putting unnecessary costs on Kiwis.

“We would also scrap wasteful bureaucracy like the Climate Change Commission and remove the artificial auction price floor so the Government can sell units at the price the market is actually willing to pay.
“And we'd return 100 per cent of the net revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund rather than giving politicians another pot of money to spend.
“At a carbon price of around $55, the ETS costs an average household an estimated $478 a year. ACT says that if New Zealanders are going to pay a carbon price, the revenue should come back to them.
“ACT will cut unnecessary costs, protect Kiwi jobs, return carbon revenue to households and let innovation deliver cleaner solutions.
“Cut the waste, grow the country, and unlock New Zealand’s potential.”
####### Law & Order
####### Rural
## Rural Crime Crackdown

Crime in rural New Zealand is growing, and too many rural communities feel like they've been left to fend for themselves. Today, ACT is announcing a new Rural Crime Policy to restore law and order to the countryside.
#### ACT will:
- ⁠Fund Police to hire more officers for rural areas with a target of an additional 100,000 extra patrol hours each year, and establish a dedicated rural crime unit.
- Extend eligibility for Text 111 services to people in rural areas with unreliable mobile coverage, ensuring they can contact emergency services via text when a voice call drops out.
- ⁠Crack down on armed poachers and livestock rustling with increased penalties and strengthened offences.
- ⁠Strengthen the tools used between agencies for rural enforcement coordination.
Federated Farmers' latest Rural Crime Survey found 67% of farmers experienced crime, up from 41% in 2016.
#### In our team’s words:

“Talk to farmers, and you'll hear the same story. Illegal hunters are crossing private land. Livestock stolen or killed. Sheds broken into. Fuel and machinery are disappearing overnight. Meanwhile, police resources have been steadily pulled out of rural communities,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.
“When people stop reporting crime because they don't believe anything will happen, that's a sign the system isn't working.
“Criminals target rural people because they’re isolated. Our policy takes that out of the equation, with more police presence, connectivity and harsher deterrents.”

ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Mark Cameron says: “When criminals know the nearest police car is miles away, they are emboldened. It is no surprise that nearly half of farmers do not even bother reporting incidents to the police, and of those who do, only 15% see the offender investigated and prosecuted.”

“Farmers deserve the same protection and peace of mind as anyone living in a city. Rural New Zealand helps feed the country and drive our economy. The least the government can do is make sure the people who live and work there feel safe in their own homes and on their own land. ACT will ensure the justice system treats rural crime with the seriousness it deserves, and put police back on the rural beat,” says Mr Hoggard.

"ACT is proud to be rural New Zealand’s authentic voice in parliament. When every other party sold rural New Zealand out with the Zero Carbon Act, ACT stood alone against it and kept campaigning to keep agriculture out of the ETS. We've achieved that in Government, we're making property rights the focus of the RMA, we've gotten rid of Labour's anti-farming policies like the ute tax, winter grazing rules and overzealous freshwater farm plans."
####### Democracy & Equal Rights
## Free Speech for Regulated Professionals

Professional regulators exist to protect the public by setting standards for competence, safety and conduct at work. They should not decide which lawful political or personal views a New Zealander is allowed to hold.

Teachers, nurses, real estate agents and other professionals have faced disciplinary action or compulsory ideological training over opinions expressed outside their work. More than 200,000 New Zealanders work in regulated professions. Their ability to earn a living should not depend on agreeing with their regulator's politics.

ACT will legislate to keep regulators focused on professional performance and public safety. Serious misconduct at work would still be punished. Lawful expression in a person's private life would not be a professional offence.
#### ACT will:
- Ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice.
- Require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues.
- Restrict mandatory training to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety.
- Strengthen judicial oversight so courts can rein in regulators that go beyond their legal powers.
- Preserve regulators' ability to act against genuine professional misconduct, harm to clients or patients, and breaches of professional duties.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Public Service spokesperson Todd Stephenson says:

“New Zealanders should not have to choose between their career and their right to free speech. If someone is competent, safe and professional at work, a regulator should not threaten their livelihood because it dislikes a lawful opinion they expressed in their own time.

“More than 200,000 people work in regulated professions. Every one of them should be able to support a political party, sign a petition, attend a peaceful protest or join a public debate without wondering whether their registration is at risk.

“ACT will require regulators to stay politically neutral, keep compulsory training tied to competence and safety, and give the courts stronger ability to stop regulatory overreach. Professionals should be judged on how they do their jobs, not whether their opinions are fashionable.”

Thursday, 10 September 2026
## Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

#### “ACT will complete the remaining historical Treaty claims, end the Waitangi Tribunal’s contemporary jurisdiction, and wind it up once its historical work is finished, ACT Leader David Seymour says.
David Seymour
“ACT will complete the remaining historical Treaty claims, end the Waitangi Tribunal’s contemporary jurisdiction, and wind it up once its historical work is finished, ACT Leader David Seymour says.

“The Waitangi Tribunal has been part of New Zealand’s constitutional landscape for more than fifty years. It has made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances. But no institution should exist just because it always has.

“ACT supports completing full and final historical Treaty settlements as a pragmatic way to resolve past injustices. This includes where the Crown confiscated land or otherwise breached property rights. That work should be finished properly.
“But the Tribunal that exists today is very different from the institution established in 1975.

“Through urgent and Kaupapa inquiries, the Tribunal now passes judgement on day-to-day government policy. It proposes alternative policy settings and seeks to steer decisions that properly belong to elected Governments and Parliament. This is not the Tribunal’s role and never was.
“As we approach 2040, two centuries since the signing of the Treaty, it is time to complete the historical settlements and move New Zealand forward.

“Every New Zealander deserves strong legal protections and access to the courts, regardless of ancestry. ACT believes those protections should be strengthened for everyone, not maintained through a permanent separate system for one group.
ACT will move New Zealand beyond the Waitangi Tribunal with four reforms:
01 Complete the historical settlement process

Every eligible historical claim before the Tribunal should be heard and resolved. ACT will limit the Tribunal to historical claims lodged by 1 September 2008. End its role in reviewing current government policy and actions. Ensure that all existing historical claims will still be heard and completed.
02 Stop the activism

New Zealanders choose policy at elections, and a parallel tribunal shouldn’t override that. After 50 years of evolution, its modern role no longer continues to serve New Zealand well. ACT will end the Waitangi Tribunal’s jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, leaving it to focus solely on completing the remaining historical claims.
03 Protect everyone’s rights through the law

No group should need a separate tribunal for rights that should be protected for everyone under ordinary law. Equally, no Government should unlawfully take property, interfere with rights, or act outside the law. Every New Zealander should be able to challenge this in our courts. ACT has already announced that we’ll add property rights to the Bill of Rights protecting everyone’s rights through law.
04 Wind up the Tribunal when the job is done

The Tribunal’s historic work is finite and nearly completed. ACT will not set an arbitrary deadline that rushes the remaining claims. ACT will amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed.

“As 2040 approaches, we should complete the remaining historical settlements, protecting every New Zealander’s right under the same law and courts, and move forward under one law for all with one future together.”

## ACT will make farming fun again

#### “I’m launching ACT’s campaign to Make Farming Fun Again, because I’ve spent more than 20 years farming and have seen first-hand what happens when people in Wellington, who don’t understand farming, try to regulate every part of it,” says ACT Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.
Andrew Hoggard

“I’m launching ACT’s campaign to Make Farming Fun Again, because I’ve spent more than 20 years farming and have seen first-hand what happens when people in Wellington, who don’t understand farming, try to regulate every part of it,” says ACT Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“There’s nothing fun about paperwork, especially when it’s pointless, yet farmers have been hit with endless new rules and freshwater regulations, Significant Natural Areas [SNAs], winter grazing, emissions pricing, the ute tax, firearms changes, health and safety paperwork, and resource management red tape. Successive governments piled on the rules, adding costs and uncertainty to running a farm.

“Farmers are exposed to risk that not many other industries are. In Wellington if there’s a heavy hail storm the bureaucrats work from home, on the farm it could mean you lose a crop and face huge losses.
“We can’t control the weather or foreign commodity prices, but we can stop the Government from causing headaches through pointless rules and red tape. That’s why I joined ACT and ran for Parliament.

“I want my daughters, if they choose farming, to have the freedom to farm well without the red tape I’ve faced for 20 years. As ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson, I cut unworkable winter grazing rules, kept farming out of the ETS by scrapping He Waka Eke Noa, halved Labour’s methane target, and killed the ute tax. We’ve simplified freshwater farm plans, put $79m into wilding pine control, restored 90-day trials, restored common sense to firearms laws, and brought common sense back to health and safety.

“Farmers do not need another politician telling them how to farm. They need a Government that respects property rights, sets clear rules around genuine environmental harm, and otherwise lets them get on with it.”
ACT has six pledges to make farming fun again:

1. Keep Wellington out of farming. Replacing the RMA is one of the biggest wins for rural New Zealand in decades. The next decisions are key for how well the new system works in practice. ACT will fight for National Policy Direction and National Standards that are clear, practical, locally responsive, and grounded in property rights.

2. Focus on practical environmentalism. Farmers have the incentives to look after their natural environment, because they depend on it for their livelihood. ACT will scrap Te Mana o te Wai and increase funding for rural catchment groups, allow targeted grazing on suitable DOC land, and carry on the war against wilding pines.

3. Keep backing farmers on climate. ACT is the only party that has never supported introducing a price on agricultural emissions. We stood alone against the Zero Carbon Act, opposed He Waka Eke Noa and successfully fought to keep agriculture out of the ETS. We will keep it that way. No other party can say this. We’ll also scrap the climate policy that adds nothing but costs to our economy, like the Net Zero target, the Climate Change Commission and the Zero Carbon Act.

4. Give farmers the tools. New Zealand farmers have always been early adopters of technology, often in spite of, not because of, the government. ACT will continue to cut red tape to make agri-innovation easier.

5. Protect rural communities. We’ll crack down on rural crime with 100,000 extra police patrol hours, harsher penalties for burglary via three strikes, an Open Seat rule so rural children can always catch the bus, and improve access to healthcare by giving pharmacists more tools to treat common ailments.

6. Grow the economy. Farmers make long-term decisions about land, stock, machinery and staff. They need stable prices, lower interest rates and confidence that Government will live within its means and stay out of commercial decisions it has no business making. No other party is prepared to make the savings in Wellington that will balance the books faster than ACT, with no new taxes.
"I’m proud of ACT’s record standing up for rural New Zealand," says ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee.

“When no other party would, we were there giving farmers a voice. Whether it was standing up for licensed firearms owners or opposing the Zero Carbon Act. Now that we’re in Government we’ve been able to make progress in fixing these issues.
"Party vote ACT to unlock the potential of rural New Zealand.”

## ACT will protect the peace, crack down on noisy vehicles
#### “ACT will crack down on noisy vehicles and increase penalties for drivers being a nuisance to neighbourhoods,” says ACT Tāmaki Candidate James Christmas.
James Christmas
“ACT will crack down on noisy vehicles and increase penalties for drivers being a nuisance to neighbourhoods,” says ACT Tāmaki Candidate James Christmas.

“I’ve knocked on thousands of doors in recent months and have heard you loud and clear in Tāmaki: you want to turn down the volume. People should be able to sleep, relax and enjoy their homes without having their street turned into someone else’s racetrack.

“I can see the attraction for boy racers to come to Tāmaki, but it’s not fair on the families and working people who have their life disrupted just because they live in a great location in a beautiful part of Auckland.

“These kinds of disturbances are already illegal, but effective enforcement can depend on a Police officer happening to be in the right place at the right time. By the time a person makes a complaint and an officer shows up on the scene, the vehicle is normally long gone.
“Technology can solve that problem, and ACT will make it happen by:
1.⁠ ⁠Introducing noise cameras. ACT will establish a fleet of relocatable noise cameras that can be deployed in communities suffering persistent problems with excessively noisy vehicles.

2.⁠ ⁠Establishing an objective and enforceable noise standard. The current law relies on a largely subjective test, which is difficult to enforce automatically. ACT will introduce a clear roadside noise limit that approved noise cameras can measure.

3.⁠ ⁠For those who want to pump up the volume, we are going to pump up the penalty. ACT will increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise by ensuring it is treated consistently, regardless of whether the noise comes from equipment inside the vehicle or from the vehicle’s engine or exhaust, and is punished appropriately.

“Hard working Kiwis shouldn't be harassed and inconvenienced by people who can’t take personal responsibility for their noise. Noise cameras enable evidence of offending to be collected the moment the offence occurs.
“Pairing technology with clear standards and real consequences will give residents the peace and quiet they deserve and ensure the comfort of many isn’t sacrificed for the noise of a few.”

Monday, 28 September 2026
## ACT’s plan to increase supermarket competition

#### “While other parties destroy investor confidence by proposing break-ups, price controls, or state-run alternatives. ACT will focus on the barriers that make it hard for new competitors to enter the New Zealand market,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour

“While other parties destroy investor confidence by proposing break-ups, price controls, or state-run alternatives. ACT will focus on the barriers that make it hard for new competitors to enter the New Zealand market,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“The disease of New Zealand politics today is cynical, focus-group driven, knee-jerk reactions to large problems. Politicians hear a complaint and try to play the hero by attacking a group of New Zealanders as the scapegoat of the hour.

“This politics erodes the trust and certainty needed for investment and innovation. It’s careless about the long-term effect on our country so long as those behind it think they’ll get a short-term political gain.

“We’ve seen it over and again these last six years as prices have risen as fast as, or faster than, wages. When petrol felt expensive, Jacinda said we were being ‘fleeced’ by the petrol stations. When rents went up, new taxes and regulations were put on landlords. When butter was in the news, it was Fonterra, then electricity companies, then banks, now supermarkets.

“None of this pile on mentality has made life more affordable. It’s usually ended with another layer of regulation and bureaucracy, such as the Grocery Commissioner and supplier code. New Zealand has simply been left divided and blame-happy by this pattern of political behaviour.

“The current pathway is too complex and too costly for entrants to take the risk. You have to deal with dozens of regulators - The Commerce Commission. MPI. WorkSafe. IRD. Customs. NZTA. The Privacy Commissioner. Police. MBIE. And then your local council. If you want to operate in more than one town, that's not one council, that's every council, each with their own rules, timelines and processes.
“And then there's resource consent. To open one new supermarket in New Zealand, on average, you are looking at two years and a million dollars before you’ve laid a brick.

“ACT would create a one-stop consenting shop for new market entrants - a single point where a business looking to open, or open multiple sites, can get their consents, their liquor licences, their approvals, in months, not years.
“A one-stop shop means the next entrepreneur who wants to build the next Kai Co doesn't need a team of consultants and two years of patience just to get out of the starting blocks.

“We’ll also change product labelling laws. Right now, anyone selling imported food not labelled for New Zealand has two options. They can do an expensive run of product packaged specifically to our regulations, or they need to unload pallets, open each box, and stick nutrition labels over each product individually. That’s why the Dr Pepper you get at the dairy has a little white sticker over the nutrition panel.

“ACT will allow food labels for trusted regulatory systems like UK, EU and US by default. This will lower the barrier to entry for international supermarkets, who will no longer need to do expensive runs of products specifically for the tiny Australasian market to open stores. ACT will roll out the welcome mat.

“We’ve seen the impact of heavy-handed intervention with the oil and gas exploration ban. When the Government signals that successful businesses can simply be broken apart, potential new entrants are less likely to invest here.

“Ironically, draconian regulations can make supermarket competition worse. We won’t get Aldi, or Coles, or Walmart to come to New Zealand if they believe it’s politically fashionable to attack their investments after a few bad polls. Already, the previous Government had to exempt Costco from supplier obligations or they wouldn’t come.
“Rather than joining the race to the bottom where we attack successful businesses, ACT’s policy is to make it easier for new businesses to come here, compete, and expand.”
####### Health
## Strengthening End of Life Choice
A terminally ill person suffering unbearably should have the final say over how and when they die.
The End of Life Choice Act has given New Zealanders that option since 2021. The Ministry of Health's first statutory review recommended 25 changes to the law.

ACT MP Todd Stephenson's End of Life Choice Amendment Bill adopts all 25. It would also remove a rule that denies access when a doctor cannot say with certainty that someone has less than six months to live.
#### ACT will:
- Implement all 25 recommendations from the Ministry of Health's statutory review of the End of Life Choice Act.
- Replace the six-month prognosis requirement with a requirement that a person has an advanced, progressive condition expected to cause death.

- Keep the other eligibility tests, including that the person is at least 18, is in an advanced state of irreversible decline, is experiencing unbearable suffering that cannot be tolerably relieved, and is competent to make an informed decision.
- Allow a limited waiver of final consent when a person has been assessed as eligible and chosen the date and time while competent, but loses capacity before that date.
- Require training for practitioners, strengthen the Registrar's oversight, and spell out their duty to check that requests are free from pressure.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“The End of Life Choice Act recognises that a person living with a terminal illness is best placed to decide how their final days should be spent. Almost 1,700 New Zealanders have now chosen an assisted death.

“The latest report also shows the safeguards are working. More than 300 applicants were found ineligible last year, and 42 people withdrew. The checks are real, and the choice remains with the patient right to the end.”
ACT MP Todd Stephenson says:

“My Bill adopts all 25 recommendations from the Ministry of Health's review. It also addresses the six-month prognosis rule, which remains the biggest barrier for terminally ill New Zealanders seeking an assisted death.

“The six-month rule has shut out people who are terminally ill, in irreversible decline, and suffering unbearably because a doctor cannot say their death will occur within six months. Death does not always follow a calendar.
“The Bill replaces that cut-off with a test based on whether a person's condition is advanced, progressive, and expected to cause death. All the other eligibility criteria remain.

“It also allows a limited waiver of final consent when someone has been assessed as eligible and chosen a date while competent, but loses capacity before that date. None of the existing safeguards are being weakened.
“New Zealanders backed the original law by almost two to one. Parliament should now have the chance to consider what we have learned from its first years in operation and make it work better.”

Todd Stephenson

ACT will continue championing New Zealanders' right to make their own healthcare decisions by supporting the End of Life Choice Amendment Bill and introducing an Advance Directives Bill in the next term of Parliament, says ACT Health spokesperson Todd Stephenson.

"ACT believes competent adults should be trusted to make deeply personal decisions about their own lives. We will keep the End of Life Choice Amendment Bill on Parliament's agenda and continue building support for sensible changes that strengthen New Zealanders' choices at the end of life.

"We will also introduce an Advance Directives Bill to provide legal clarity so New Zealanders can have confidence their healthcare wishes will be respected if they are ever unable to communicate them. Thursday, 27 August 2026
## Landmark social media settlement shows better way forward

#### “ACT welcomes the changes Meta has agreed to make to its social media platforms in the United States. We are calling on Meta and all similar companies to treat New Zealand children the same as they will be required to treat American children,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour

“ACT welcomes the changes Meta has agreed to make to its social media platforms in the United States. We are calling on Meta and all similar companies to treat New Zealand children the same as they will be required to treat American children,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
“Protecting children online is a serious problem, that’s why ACT pushed for Parliament to investigate the issue. We are now seeing a genuine, realistic solution take shape.

“As part of a settlement with US states, Meta has agreed to make significant changes to its platforms. These include a default two-hour daily limit for teenagers, locking most teen accounts between midnight and 6am, switching off push notifications overnight and during school hours, and giving parents greater power to supervise and restrict their children’s accounts. Teenagers would also need parental approval to loosen the main restrictions.

“The best thing the New Zealand Government could do for young New Zealanders is tell Meta we want to have the same settings here, and challenge other major social media companies to match them. That would be a more effective and realistic solution than implementing a ban which won’t work and is fraught with unintended consequences.

“The problem with these bans is that teenagers are smarter and more determined at using the internet than adults. Anything strict enough to stop motivated teenagers will affect adult freedom, but teenagers will drive a bus through anything loose enough to not affect adults.

“Instead of pretending teenagers can simply be kept off social media because politicians say so, it changes the features that encourage excessive use, gives parents greater control, and puts responsibility on the companies designing the platforms.

“Before Parliament creates another bureaucracy with unintended consequences, imposes widespread online identification, starts restricting legitimate privacy tools, or threatens companies with fines they’ll never pay, we should look to implement the solution right in front of us.”

## Campaign launched to acquire land for new school in Epsom

#### “I will be campaigning for the Government to acquire the University of Auckland Epsom Campus for educational purposes, creating a new school to serve the community,” says MP for Epsom David Seymour.
David Seymour
“I will be campaigning for the Government to acquire the University of Auckland Epsom Campus for educational purposes, creating a new school to serve the community,” says MP for Epsom David Seymour.

“This project will protect the existing Grammar zones by creating a new education option without changing the zoning. If the land is not used for a new school, the substantial land that the University is selling will be developed into high density housing, exacerbating the immense pressure already on the existing Grammar zones.

“I have been engaged on the future of this land since at least 2019, when I first met with the University about their plan to exit the Epsom Campus. I have primarily been concerned with ensuring the two existing schools at the southern end, Auckland Normal Intermediate and Kohia Terrace School, do not lose their fields or walkable access. The Ministry of Education has been in negotiations to secure at least that much land.
“However, new developments have shifted my focus to acquiring the land in its entirety, something I previously did not think possible or affordable.

“In July I was approached by the Principals of Auckland Grammar School and Epsom Girls’ Grammar school. They and their boards would like to co-sponsor a co-educational high school on the land, initially using the existing buildings.
“Since their approach, I have sought assurance from the Minister of Education the land will not be sold in the immediate future.

“The support of Mrs McNaughton and Mr O’Connor means the school would be backed by two of the country’s greatest educators. It would be the only co-educational school in the area, something I know some parents would prefer for their children.
“It would be a school of excellence, taking pressure off the existing schools without removing the entitlement for those in zone to attend the traditional Grammars if they wish to.

“The cost of the land is substantial, I have also asked the Minister to investigate other land holdings the Ministry of Education has that might be sold to cover the cost. For example, the Ministry bought a substantial piece beside Alexandra Park in the 1990s that has not been used.

“The school should be unzoned and accept students from across the city. Taking pressure off Mt Albert Grammar that is successful to bursting point. It also fulfils the original Auckland Grammar ethos, ‘for persons of all classes and races who may inhabit this colony.’

“The continued use of the land for education would ensure that the property remains open, green space. Everyone accepts that central Auckland will intensify over time, but more terraced housing and apartments makes it even more important that green spaces and local facilities like schools are provided.

“This land and its future use are not only important to the Epsom community, but families across the Auckland region who want a quality education. Whoever forms the next Government, I will be taking it to them as a critical project for our community and those surrounding it.”

## Leave spirituality out of infrastructure

#### "New Zealanders should be able to build a house, a solar farm or a factory without being made to take part in, or pay for, a religious ceremony as a condition of consent," says ACT’s Infrastructure, Energy and Climate Change spokesperson, Simon Court.
Simon Court

New Zealanders should be able to build a house, a solar farm or a factory without being made to take part in, or pay for, a religious ceremony as a condition of consent," says ACT’s Infrastructure, Energy and Climate Change spokesperson, Simon Court.

Planning law should regulate effects that can be identified, measured and tested, and protect rights recognised by law. It should not require planners, councils or judges to rule on spiritual or religious beliefs.
"Unfortunately, emerging litigation has seen spiritual effects increasingly become part of our resource management system.

“For example, some housing developments must invite iwi to perform a karakia before construction begins, with the developer paying for it. IKEA’s Sylvia Park consent requires invitations to seven mana whenua groups to attend karakia and ceremonies at specified construction milestones. Solar farms at Ongaonga and Ōpunake have similar conditions. The Ōtākiri water-bottling dispute reached the Supreme Court, where evidence about te mauri o te wai was considered.

“The new Planning Act and Natural Environment Act, which received Royal assent this week, are a significant improvement. They do not carry over the RMA’s spiritual-value requirement. But leaving a requirement out is not the same as ruling it out. Without a clear boundary, people can still bring spiritual matters back in under broader cultural-effects provisions, leaving councils and courts to draw the line case by case.
“ACT will finish the job.”
ACT will:

- Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects. A religious or spiritual belief, or a claim of spiritual harm, could not on its own be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information, or imposing a consent condition. The rule would apply equally to all religions and belief systems and use the test already applied under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act.

- Ban compulsory spiritual observances. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or fund a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. Anyone who wants to do these things voluntarily still could.
- Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes. Councils would work to clear, testable standards for water quality, ecosystem health and human health.

"None of this takes away protection for anything real. Heritage sites, urupā, archaeological sites, customary physical uses, water quality, ecosystems and rights in Treaty settlement legislation would all still be dealt with directly.

"The test is simple. Is there an identifiable physical effect, place, resource or legal right? If there is, deal with it. If the claimed effect exists only as a spiritual proposition, it isn't the planning system's job."

Wednesday, 7 October 2026
## ACT will remove the cap on generosity

#### “If New Zealanders want to give to a good cause they should be encouraged to do so. ACT’s Fiscal Plan, released on Sunday, will do away with the $33,333 cap on the tax benefits available for charitable donations,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour

“If New Zealanders want to give to a good cause they should be encouraged to do so. ACT’s Fiscal Plan, released on Sunday, will do away with the $33,333 cap on the tax benefits available for charitable donations,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
“A small number of generous donors have changed lives for an enormous number of Kiwis. Their generosity should be welcomed, not punished.

“Just look at the good these donations bring about. In Wellington a brand-new children’s hospital has opened, this wouldn’t have been possible without the generosity of Sir Mark Dunajtschik and Dame Dorothy Spotswood.

“Starship is another example of what New Zealand can achieve, and it wouldn’t be possible without the kindness of people who are willing to give some of what they’ve earned to help someone else live a better life.

“ACT’s plan for New Zealand’s first Comprehensive Cancer Centre will also be achieved by partnering with New Zealand’s leading philanthropists, families, businesses, charitable trusts, community organisations and successful Kiwis, we can build something extraordinary.

“If New Zealanders want to give $1 million, $10 million or more to cancer care, medical research or other causes, the tax system should encourage that generosity, not impose an arbitrary ceiling on it.
“On Sunday ACT will release its fiscal plan. It will remove locks on New Zealand’s potential like the charities cap, and it will get rid of the waste that prevents us from growing the economy.”
####### Press Release
Friday, 9 October 2026
## Keep agriculture in the curriculum
#### “ACT will campaign for agriculture to remain a subject in the Year 11 school curriculum,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.
Andrew Hoggard
“ACT will campaign for agriculture to remain a subject in the Year 11 school curriculum,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“In September, I wrote to Education Minister Erica Stanford asking her to confirm that Agricultural and Horticultural Science will remain as a standalone subject in the Year 11 Science curriculum. I’m gutted to learn this isn’t the case.
“We’re a food and fibre producing nation so learning about our biggest exporter shouldn’t be an unconventional subject.

“Food and fibre exports are forecast to reach $64.3 billion in the year to June 2026, we should encourage more young Kiwis to learn the ropes, but interest will shrink if we don’t make it easily available.

“Over the last nine years 111,693 have studied Agricultural and Horticultural Science across 359 schools. 63 percent of students taking the subject are at urban schools. It is not only rural students who benefit, for many young people in towns and cities this may be their only structured chance to learn how the industry works.

“Removing agriculture as a Year 11 standalone subject sends the wrong message. For schools with strong agricultural programmes – such as Feilding High School, which recently featured on Country Calendar – this change creates a real challenge for them, by leaving a gap in their Year 11 programme.

“It’s also an industry loaded with well-paying jobs if only talented young Kiwis would take them. Given that dance is a standalone subject at Year 11, I don't understand why schools that already have a programme, and have a student demand for it, can't have the opportunity to teach it."

Saturday, 10 October 2026
## New Zealand can't keep exporting taxpayers' money
#### “New Zealand is in the sh*t, can we seriously afford to be sending millions of dollars overseas for tripe like ‘climate-smart’ passionfruit?” asks ACT list candidate Paul Henry.
Paul Henry
“New Zealand is in the sh*t, can we seriously afford to be sending millions of dollars overseas for tripe like ‘climate-smart’ passionfruit?” asks ACT list candidate Paul Henry.
“ACT will cut wasteful and low-priority MFAT spending, focus New Zealand’s aid on our national interests, and make every programme prove its value to taxpayers.

“New Zealand has good reason to spend overseas – a stable, prosperous Pacific, strong trade ties and the ability to help when disaster strikes. But foreign aid is taxpayers’ money, and should face the same scrutiny as spending here at home.
“Here’s an uncomfortable truth, our economy is too small. Our bureaucracy is too big. We cannot spend our way to prosperity. We need to be disciplined if we’re to get the books back in order.
“ACT will reduce foreign aid to 2017 levels, excluding support for Ukraine. This will save around $283 million a year.

“Since 2024, MFAT spent $15 million on developing countries to prepare for the Paris Agreement – an agreement that is broken and cannot accommodate targets that reflect the real warming impact of New Zealand’s emissions.

“Nearly $21 million was spent on sustainable agriculture investment in Africa; $6.3 million to develop different crops in Timor-Lester; $6.2 million on supporting gender diversity for Climate-Smart Passionfruit chain in Viet Nam; $5.1 million to Timor-Leste to publish three educational magazines – I could go on, but just like we don’t have the money for this nonsense, I don’t have the heartbeats for it either.
“That’s already around $50 million for other countries and their pet projects. This is absolutely barking mad.

“ACT will be campaigning to give MFAT a reality check on behalf of taxpayers. We cannot afford this kind of spending when our own country is paying an eye-watering debt – a debt that already costs us almost $25 million a day just in interest payments.

“If nothing changes, the best-case scenario is our grandchildren will still be paying the interest on our debt. Worst-case the Greens get in and then it will be our great, great, great grandchildren’s problem as well.

“I didn’t stand for ACT for something to do. I stood because I believe in New Zealand’s extraordinary potential – and I won’t stand by while taxpayers’ money goes to solving other countries’ problems before our own.
“ACT wants to invigorate New Zealand with the aspiration and ambition the country was once world famous for. Party Vote ACT to cut the waste and grow the country.”

## ACT to abolish another of Labour's renters' taxes
#### “ACT is campaigning to reverse another of Labour’s renters’ taxes by abolishing loss ring-fencing for rental properties,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
David Seymour
“ACT is campaigning to reverse another of Labour’s renters’ taxes by abolishing loss ring-fencing for rental properties,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.
“Median weekly rents rose by $180 during Labour’s time in government. Labour claimed it was helping renters, then made it more expensive to provide the homes they live in.

“There’s no such thing as a tax on landlords that renters can safely ignore. When Labour made rental housing more expensive to provide, tenants faced the consequences through pressure on rents, fewer homes, less choice, and poorer quality.

“ACT will allow residential rental losses incurred from the day the policy takes effect to be offset against other taxable income. This will apply to existing homes and new builds. Losses already ring-fenced will remain subject to the existing rules.

“If you’re a sole trader or make other investments, such as commercial property, your losses can be offset against your personal income. ACT’s proposal levels the playing field and ensures treatment is consistent.

“Labour’s policy meant legitimate losses could not be offset when cashflow is tightest, forcing landlords to wait until a property became profitable – when cashflow relief is needed least. If cashflow is tight, it’s much harder to carry out essential repairs if the tax deduction is delayed for years.
“The only way to secure more affordable housing for renters is to build more homes and reduce the costs that get passed through to renters.

“Removing ring-fencing will improve the viability of rental investment, including investment in new homes. Alongside ACT’s resource management reforms and opening up access to new building materials, it will encourage supply and give renters more choice.

“Expect the usual cries of ‘tax cuts for landlords’. Labour played the same cynical game when the Government restored mortgage interest deductibility, yet with ACT in Government and rents flatlining, it's renters who have reaped the benefits. Nearly three years on, Labour has come to its senses and decided not to reverse ACT’s change.

“Our policy brings tax relief forward for losses that would eventually be deducted under the current rules. It doesn’t increase the total deduction. But some losses may never be used, and earlier deductions reduce government revenue in the meantime. So, we can’t say the policy has no fiscal cost.
“We estimated the cost by reversing the impact of the rules when the Government introduced them, consistent with Treasury’s approach.
“The policy is forecast to reduce government revenue by $264 million in year one, rising to $303 million in year four, and is accounted for in ACT’s fully-costed fiscal plan.”

## Harsher penalties for trashing communities
#### “ACT will increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping, and punish anyone using the land as their personal tip," says ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.
Andrew Hoggard
“ACT will increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping, and punish anyone using the land as their personal tip," says ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.
"Illegal dumping is vandalism by another name. It's unfair on ratepayers, damaging to the environment, and shows a complete disregard for people who take pride in their communities.

“Communities are being forced to foot the bill for this behaviour. Thousands of tonnes of illegally dumped waste are collected every year, with clean-up costs running into the millions. That cost ends up being borne out of ratepayers' backpocket.

"Every mattress dumped on a roadside, every trailer-load of rubbish abandoned, and every pile of waste thrown into a ditch ends up becoming someone else's problem, both from the costs to clean it up and the effect on the land. Dumped rubbish can contaminate streams, harm livestock, attract pests, and create fire hazards.
"Anyone who thinks that is acceptable needs to face the kinds of consequences that will make them reconsider.

“ACT will increase the infringement fee for illegal dumping from $400 to $1,000, with repeat offenders facing fines of $2,000. For the most serious offences, courts will have the power to impose higher penalties.

“In my own community, I've come home to find someone had walked down to the local river to burn a pile of nappies, glass bottles, and tin cans. They did this right beside our favourite swimming hole and a spot where the local primary school comes to learn about river ecology.
“The current $400 penalty isn't cutting it. If you're prepared to dump rubbish beside a river, and leave someone else to deal with the mess, a slap on the wrist isn't much of a deterrent.
"It's not good enough that hard-working families are left paying the price for people who think the roadside or a rural area is their personal tip.

"Most New Zealanders do the right thing. They pay for rubbish collection, use transfer stations, and follow the rules. For those who don't, stronger penalties send a simple message: if you dump your rubbish illegally, you'll face consequences."

## ACT will invest $400 million to get Kiwis more GP appointments

#### “ACT will invest an additional $400 million in general practice over four years to keep doctors in New Zealand, attract more from overseas, and deliver more GP appointments,” says ACT Candidate for Tāmaki James Christmas.
James Christmas

“ACT will invest an additional $400 million in general practice over four years to keep doctors in New Zealand, attract more from overseas, and deliver more GP appointments,” says ACT Candidate for Tāmaki James Christmas.

“Too many New Zealanders can’t get a GP appointment when they need one. In 2024/25, one in four adults and one in five children missed a GP visit because the wait was too long. That means parents worrying about sick children, people putting off treatment, and patients ending up in emergency departments unnecessarily.

“Labour’s policy to hand out three taxpayer-funded GP visits each year for the worried well will only make things worse. There’s no point promising more free appointments if there aren’t enough doctors to provide them.
“Rather than subsidising demand, ACT will increase the supply of appointments by keeping the doctors we’ve got, helping them see more patients, and attracting more from overseas.
1. Keep GPs working and in New Zealand

“The easiest doctor to recruit is the one you don’t lose. With 35 per cent of GPs intending to retire within five years and 18 per cent considering moving overseas, we need to make it more attractive for them to stay.
“ACT’s funding will help practices offer competitive remuneration, retain experienced staff, and encourage doctors to remain in practice rather than retire early or move overseas.
2. Help GPs see more patients
“We don’t have to wait for a new generation of doctors to graduate. We can make better use of the workforce we already have.

“GPs work an average of 33.9 hours a week, down from 36.4 a decade ago, while nearly one in ten works 19 hours or fewer. Restoring average hours to previous levels would be equivalent to hundreds of additional full-time doctors, without recruiting a single new GP.
“Not every GP can or wants to work more hours. But better funding could help practices offer extra hours, reward additional appointments, and encourage experienced doctors to keep working longer.
3. Attract qualified doctors from overseas

“We cannot afford to turn away qualified doctors because of unnecessary red tape. Work is already underway to streamline registration for overseas-trained medical professionals, including new fast-track pathways for qualified GPs.

“ACT will build on that progress by reforming and streamlining medical regulators to focus on getting safe, competent professionals into the health system, rather than putting unnecessary obstacles in their way.

“Unlocking New Zealand's potential means making sure poor health doesn't hold people back. Combined with ACT’s plans to close the medicines gap with Australia, introduce Pharmacy First, and establish a world-class cancer centre, ACT has the most credible and comprehensive plan to improve healthcare for New Zealanders.”
The funding will be an ongoing $100 million annual boost to general practice, on top of normal capitation increases, totalling $400 million over the first four years.

blocks: ## One Law for All. One Future Together.
#### One law for all means the same rights, the same duties, and the same protection under the law.
## One Law for All.
#### New Zealand should be a country where everyone is equal before the law, Parliament makes the law, Government is bound by the law, and the property people work hard for is secure.
#### These are basic foundations of a free and democratic country. But over time, vague Treaty clauses and expanding judicial interpretations have blurred who gets to make the rules.
#### ACT will:
#### Ensure Parliament Makes the Rules
Enshrine in the Constitution Act that Parliament makes the law, Government is bound by it, and every New Zealander is equal before it.
#### Protect Property Rights
Protect your home, farm, business, and other property by adding property rights to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
#### Rein in the Activist Courts
Stop courts using broad Treaty interpretations to impose obligations Parliament never actually legislated.
#### Require Clarity When Referring to the Treaty
Make Parliament say clearly what it means when it refers to the Treaty, instead of leaving courts and officials to fill in the gaps.
#### Join the Campaign for Equal Rights
###### Submit
###### Submit
## One Public Service.

#### Previous governments spent years building separate tracks for different groups, and too many of those rules remain. ACT will remove them and build one public service with one standard for everyone.
#### ACT will:
#### End race-based hiring.

Government jobs should go to the best candidate, whoever they are. But the law still tells public employers to shape employment policies around the aspirations and employment needs of particular ethnic groups. ACT will repeal those rules in section 73 of the Public Service Act and section 118 of the Crown Entities Act. Laws against discrimination and unsafe workplaces will remain. So will the rule that public service appointments must be based on merit.
#### Keep spiritual practices voluntary.

Taxpayer money isn’t for running spiritual or religious activities at work. ACT will end the use of public time and public funds for this, whatever the tradition. Staff will remain free to practise their own religion, culture, or traditions in their own time, and workplaces can make reasonable arrangements for them.
#### Rewrite the Public Service Act.

ACT will make these changes straight away, then rewrite the Act so the public service stays politically neutral, hires on merit, treats people equally, and is judged on whether services actually reach the people who need them.
#### Deliver public services based on need, not race.

ACT will put into law that public services should go to the people who need them, whoever they are. If two New Zealanders have the same need, government should treat them the same. The Government has already told agencies to follow that rule. ACT will put it in law so people can challenge decisions that break it in court.
#### Remove cultural tests that have nothing to do with the job.

Job ads should ask whether you can do the work, not whether you know the right cultural concepts or share the right worldview. ACT will tell agencies to remove these requirements from job ads and position descriptions unless the knowledge is actually needed for the job.
## Free Speech for All.

#### Professional regulators exist to protect the public by setting standards for competence, safety and conduct at work. They should not decide which lawful political or personal views a New Zealander is allowed to hold.
#### ACT will:
#### Protect Lawful Expression
Ban professional regulators from disciplining members for lawful expression outside their professional practice.
#### Ensure Neutrality
Require regulators to remain institutionally neutral on political and ideological issues.
#### Axe Irrelevant Training
Restrict mandatory training to matters directly connected to professional competence and public safety.
#### Strengthen Judicial Oversight
Strengthen judicial oversight so courts can rein in regulators that go beyond their legal powers.
#### Preserve Regulators Core Purpose
Preserve regulators' ability to act against genuine professional misconduct, harm to clients or patients, and breaches of professional duties.
## Our Record.
#### In Government, ACT has driven major changes toward equal rights, democratic accountability and a politically neutral public service.
#### Making need, not race, the rule for public services
ACT secured a Cabinet circular directing agencies to target services according to individual need instead of using ethnicity as a proxy.
#### Removing race-based institutions and legal duties

The Government abolished the Māori Health Authority, removed race-based requirements from health law and repealed section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act so decisions focus on children's safety and wellbeing.
#### Restoring local democracy

ACT secured the return of binding local referendums on Māori wards. The Government has also adopted the substance of Cameron Luxton's Member's Bill so unelected council appointees will no longer be able to vote or count toward quorum under the Local Government Act.
#### Putting merit and neutrality back into the public service

The Public Service Amendment Act reinforces political neutrality, merit-based appointments and professional competence, and removes statutory requirements to pursue demographic representation in public-service employment.
#### Ending race-based procurement targets
ACT secured the removal of the target requiring eight per cent of government contracts to be awarded to Māori-owned businesses. Public contracts should be awarded on value and performance.
#### Protecting liberties and property rights in lawmaking

The Regulatory Standards Act requires new laws to be assessed openly against principles including personal liberty, property rights, equality before the law and good legislative process. An independent Regulatory Standards Board can examine complaints and report publicly.
#### Stopping state-backed speech policing

The Government halted Labour's proposed hate-speech expansion and agreed to disestablish the Broadcasting Standards Authority after ACT challenged its attempt to extend broadcasting rules to podcasts and online media.
#### The coalition Government has not gone as far as ACT would like, but it has gone further than it would have without ACT.
## Fighting for a free, fair and equal New Zealand.
#### We are proud to represent ACT’s values of freedom, personal responsibility, and opportunity for all New Zealanders.

The people who exercise public power should answer to voters, and taxpayers should be able to see who is responsible when government fails. ACT stands for one person, one vote and one law for all. We will enshrine equal rights in the Constitution Act, protect lawful speech from professional regulators, put funding for human rights into resolving real cases, and make central government small enough for ministers to be held accountable. ## Expanding Charter Schools

The right school can change a child’s life. Charter schools give families more choice and educators the freedom to teach in ways that work for their students. Some cater for children with autism; others support high performance athletes. That freedom comes with clear standards for attendance and achievement, and schools can be shut down if they don’t deliver.

ACT brought charter schools back, and more than 2,000 students are already enrolled. We will protect them from Labour’s plans to shut them down and expand enrolments to 10,000 by the end of 2029, with the goal of a charter school option in every major town.
### ACT will:
- Protect charter schools from Labour’s plans to shut them down.
- Set a target of 10,000 charter school enrolments by the end of 2029, with annual reporting on progress.
- Help more suitable state and state-integrated schools convert to charter schools by removing unnecessary barriers relating to employment, property and funding.
- Encourage new charter schools where there is sufficient demand and a suitable sponsor, with the goal of a charter school option in every major town.
- Manage funding for growth transparently through existing education budgets.
- Retain strong performance standards for attendance, achievement, financial management and student wellbeing, with schools held accountable for results.
### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:
“When schools are given greater freedom to innovate and respond to the needs of their students, families benefit and students thrive.
“Families have deliberately chosen to move outside the traditional system because it was not meeting their needs. Hipkins is saying Labour would force them back in.
“Charter schools cost less to establish than equivalent state schools, and are accountable to deliver results – they can be shut down if they don’t.”

## A Real Pathway to a Trade

Too many young New Zealanders are pushed towards university without being given a proper chance to try a trade. For a bright, ambitious young person, an apprenticeship can mean earning while they learn and building skills that could one day lead to running a business of their own.

ACT will end the university-first mindset and put trades on an equal footing. We’ll build a proper national pathway so choosing a trade is just as straightforward and respected as choosing university.
Read ACT's full policy here.
#### ACT will:
- Remove funding caps on approved trades subjects at school, with funding following students and schools keeping their base and equity funding when students learn off-site.
- Create Industry Awards alongside University Entrance, showing employers that students have completed relevant learning and are ready for their next step.
- Give employers a stronger voice in what students learn, with Industry Skills Boards developing new subjects as technology and workforce needs change.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT List Candidate Paul Henry says:

"Trades are not a second-best option. For a bright, ambitious young person, becoming an electrician, builder, or mechanic can be the most intelligent decision they ever make. They can earn while they learn, build valuable skills, avoid taking on a large student loan, and potentially go on to run their own business and employ others.
“ACT will end the university-first mindset and put trades on an equal footing."
####### Health
## Shorter Waits for your GP

When you’re worried about your health or a sick child, the last thing you need is a long wait for a GP. ACT will invest an extra $400 million in general practice over four years to keep experienced doctors here and help them see more patients. We’ll also cut unnecessary red tape for qualified GPs coming from overseas, so you and your family can get care sooner.
#### ACT will:
- Provide an ongoing $100 million annual boost to general practice, on top of normal capitation increases, totalling $400 million over the first four years.

- Keep experienced GPs working and in New Zealand by helping practices offer competitive remuneration and retain staff, making it more attractive for doctors to stay rather than retire early or move overseas.
- Help GPs see more patients by supporting practices to offer extra hours and reward additional appointments, so doctors who want to can see more patients and stay in practice longer.
- Attract qualified doctors from overseas by reforming and streamlining medical regulators so safe, competent professionals can enter the health system sooner.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Candidate for Tāmaki James Christmas says:
“There’s no point promising more free appointments if there aren’t enough doctors to provide them.

“The easiest doctor to recruit is the one you don’t lose. With 35 per cent of GPs intending to retire within five years and 18 per cent considering moving overseas, we need to make it more attractive for them to stay.”
####### Education
## Fair Funding for Independent Schools

The right school can change a child’s future. Parents who choose an independent school often make real sacrifices to pay the fees, while still paying taxes towards education. ACT will keep independent school funding in step with increases for state schools, helping ease pressure on fees so families can keep choosing the education that suits their child.
#### ACT will:
- Increase the independent school subsidy by the same percentage as state school operational funding in every future Budget.
- Retain the roll-growth funding changes secured in Budget 2025, so funding continues to adjust as more children attend independent schools.

A two per cent increase in state school operational funding would mean a two per cent increase in the independent school subsidy. Schools would have more certainty as they plan ahead, instead of seeing their support stay at the same dollar figure for years.
####### Law & Order
## Tougher Penalties for Rubbish Dumping

The people trashing our communities are leaving ratepayers with the bill. ACT will raise fines for illegal rubbish dumping to $1,000, and $2,000 for repeat offenders, to protect roadsides and rivers and make offenders think twice.
#### ACT will:
- Increase the infringement fee for illegal rubbish dumping from $400 to $1,000.
- Set fines of $2,000 for repeat offenders.
- Give courts the power to impose higher penalties for the most serious offences.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Rural Communities spokesperson Andrew Hoggard says:
“Illegal dumping is vandalism by another name. It's unfair on ratepayers, damaging to the environment, and shows a complete disregard for people who take pride in their communities.
“The current $400 penalty isn't cutting it. If you're prepared to dump rubbish beside a river, and leave someone else to deal with the mess, a slap on the wrist isn't much of a deterrent.”
####### Economy & Cost of Living
## Abolish Labour’s Rental Tax

Labour claimed to help renters, then made the homes they live in more expensive to provide. ACT will reverse another of Labour’s renters’ taxes by ending loss ring-fencing. This will ease pressure on rents, freeing up money for repairs and investment in more homes, and ultimately give renters more choice and market power.
#### ACT will:
- End loss ring-fencing for future rental losses. Allow residential rental losses incurred from the day the policy takes effect to be offset against other taxable income.
- Cover existing homes and new builds. Improve the viability of rental investment, including investment in new homes.
- Retain the current treatment of earlier losses. Losses already ring-fenced will remain subject to the existing rules.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“There’s no such thing as a tax on landlords that renters can safely ignore. When Labour made rental housing more expensive to provide, tenants faced the consequences through pressure on rents, fewer homes, less choice, and poorer quality.

“Removing ring-fencing will improve the viability of rental investment, including investment in new homes. Alongside ACT’s resource management reforms and opening up access to new building materials, it will encourage supply and give renters more choice.”
####### Economy & Cost of Living
## ACT's Fiscal Plan

New Zealanders are working hard, but wages aren’t stretching far enough and too many young Kiwis see a better future overseas. Making life more affordable means growing wages as well as bringing costs down. That requires confidence to invest and build businesses here.

Government has to do its part by living within its means. Taxpayers are spending more than $1 million an hour on interest alone, money that could fund better healthcare or be left in your pocket. Cutting taxes by borrowing more would only pass the bill to the next generation, with interest.

ACT’s Fiscal Plan balances the books without new taxes and starts paying down debt. We’ll cut spending outside protected frontline services and make government smaller and more accountable, with 19 departments and 18 ministers. We’ll also gradually raise the NZ Super age to 67 by 2035, with compassionate early access for people who have spent much of their careers in physically demanding jobs.

The savings let us fund better services, including easier access to care through pharmacists, and remove tax on qualifying KiwiSaver investment earnings. More of your returns can stay invested and grow for retirement, without asking you to give up more of your pay today.

By 2031, debt will be $12.4 billion lower than current forecasts, leaving New Zealand better prepared for the next earthquake or major crisis. Balancing the books lays the groundwork for much lower, flatter taxes backed by lasting spending control. We’ll cut the waste to grow the country, Lock Labour Out and Unlock New Zealand’s Potential.
### ACT’s Fiscal Plan 2026
Our plan to unlock New Zealand's potential sets out how we’ll cut waste and fund better services, with the costings in full.
#### Explore ACT’s Fiscal Plan →
### Watch New Zealand’s debt grow
See how fast New Zealand’s debt is growing and the bill taxpayers are left to carry. Our debt ticker shows the scale of the challenge.
#### Watch the debt grow →
### ACT will:
- Balance the books with no new taxes, putting much lower taxes within reach.
- Cut $9.5 billion a year from spending outside welfare and protected frontline services once fully implemented.
- Make government smaller and more accountable, with 19 departments and 18 ministers responsible for budgets and results.
- Remove tax on KiwiSaver investment earnings and discontinue the government contribution.
- Introduce a Carbon Tax Refund, returning net revenue from Emissions Trading Scheme auctions to New Zealanders.
- Gradually raise the NZ Super age to 67 by 2035, with compassionate early access for people who have spent much of their careers in physically demanding jobs.
- Fund better healthcare, expanding pharmacist care and setting aside around $2 billion as a funding contingency for a National Cancer Centre.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“It is immoral to keep borrowing for political promises and sending the bill to the next generation. We are cutting waste, bringing the surplus forward, and using some of those savings to let New Zealanders build greater financial security.

“New Zealand needs a credible path to surplus without new taxes, and an economy where work, saving and investment pay off. A stronger ACT presence in government will provide the determination to deliver both. That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential.”
####### Economy & Cost of Living
## Unlocking Mineral Wealth
New Zealand is sitting on valuable mineral and energy resources while importing more of what a modern economy needs and watching skilled Kiwis leave for mining jobs overseas.

ACT wants New Zealand to build things again. We will make it easier to responsibly develop the resources beneath our feet, bringing investment into our regions, creating high-paying careers at home, strengthening our energy and economic security, and earning royalties for New Zealanders.
Read our full policy, Unlocking Mineral and Energy Wealth, here.
#### ACT will:
- Keep New Zealand open to responsible mineral exploration and development, with the Critical Minerals List updated as new opportunities emerge.
- Establish clear national rules for mines, quarries and mineral processing, while continuing to protect national parks and Schedule 4 land.
- Keep fast-track consenting available for eligible projects and establish clear deadlines for government decisions.
- Open exploration and extraction on suitable government-owned land outside protected areas under clear and predictable rules.
- Keep onshore and offshore petroleum exploration open where commercially viable opportunities emerge.
- Remove unnecessary barriers to domestic gas production, underground gas storage and reliable thermal generation.
- Cut duplicated approval processes so companies are not forced to prove the same thing repeatedly to different regulators.
- Make regulatory requirements proportionate to the actual scale and risk of a project.
- Protect legitimate investment from arbitrary political reversals and strengthen property rights.
- Require mining and petroleum operators to pay for rehabilitation, decommissioning and ongoing treatment, rather than leaving taxpayers with the cleanup bill.
- Work with industry and training providers so more New Zealanders can build skilled, well-paid careers in the resources sector without moving overseas.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Energy and Resources spokesperson Simon Court says:

“New Zealand has minerals needed for roads, homes, power lines, phones, batteries, and medical technology. We use these products every day, but too often refuse to produce the raw materials ourselves. That does not stop mining globally. It just sends the jobs, investment and environmental responsibility offshore.

“Developing these resources responsibly creates well-paid regional jobs, supports new industries, strengthens domestic supply chains, provides strategic resources to our allies, and generates royalties for the Crown.”
