####### Infrastructure
## Leave Spirituality out of Infrastructure

New Zealanders who put their own money into building homes and businesses deserve clear rules and respect for their property rights. Yet getting consent can mean paying for compulsory karakia or answering claims of spiritual harm. ACT will keep religion out of planning decisions, giving people greater freedom to build and invest in New Zealand’s future.
#### ACT will:

- Exclude purely spiritual and religious effects from consenting. A belief or claim of spiritual harm could not, on its own, be treated as an adverse effect or justify refusing or restricting consent, requesting further information or imposing conditions. The same rule would apply to every religion and belief system.

- Ban compulsory religious observances in consent conditions. No consent or permit could require anyone to perform, take part in, arrange or pay for a prayer, karakia, blessing or other religious observance. People would remain free to do so voluntarily.
- Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes. Councils would work to clear, testable standards for water quality, ecosystem health and human health.
### In our team’s words:
ACT’s Infrastructure, Energy and Climate Change spokesperson Simon Court says:

"None of this takes away protection for anything real. Heritage sites, urupā, archaeological sites, customary physical uses, water quality, ecosystems and rights in Treaty settlement legislation would all still be dealt with directly.

"The test is simple. Is there an identifiable physical effect, place, resource or legal right? If there is, deal with it. If the claimed effect exists only as a spiritual proposition, it isn't the planning system's job."
####### Economy & Cost of Living
## No Tax on KiwiSaver Earnings

A lifetime of work and saving should give you the freedom to enjoy retirement. Yet the Government takes a cut of your KiwiSaver earnings every year, leaving less of your money to grow for the years ahead.
ACT will reward saving by letting you keep those earnings. You’ll be able to build a bigger nest egg for the retirement you want, without giving up more of the pay you need today.
Try our calculator to see how much you'd save.
Read our full policy, No tax on KiwiSaver earnings, here.
#### ACT will:
- Remove tax on qualifying investment earnings inside KiwiSaver funds, allowing your returns to stay invested and grow tax-free.
- End the annual Government Contribution for members receiving employer contributions, replacing it with tax relief on their KiwiSaver earnings.
- Put safeguards in place to keep KiwiSaver focused on retirement saving and prevent it being used to shelter large existing investment portfolios from tax.
#### In our team’s word’s:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“Other parties want to force your money into KiwiSaver, then tax you. ACT says it should be your choice, but if you save for the future we will let you get the full benefit of compounding returns instead of taxing you every step of the way.
“Every time you get taxed on your earnings you don’t just lose that money, but all the future savings that would be compounded from it.
“A country builds wealth when more people own assets, have savings, invest in productive enterprise and have the confidence to think decades ahead."

## Open the Door to Supermarket Competition

The weekly shop is expensive enough without Government making it harder for another supermarket to open. Kiwis need more businesses competing for their custom and giving them a reason to shop elsewhere.

Before a new competitor sells its first bottle of milk, it has to navigate approvals from councils and government agencies. Open in several towns and the local requirements change each time. Alcohol licensing can hold up an opening. Imported food may need special packaging or a sticker on every item before it can be sold here.
Those costs favour the businesses already here. ACT will make it easier for new supermarkets to open and grow, s shoppers have more places to take their business.
#### ACT will:

- Create a one-stop consenting shop. Bring the consents, licences and other approvals needed to open stores into one coordinated process, including when a business wants to open across multiple council areas. The aim is to get decisions in months, rather than years.
- Make alcohol licensing faster and simpler. Deal with applications earlier, instead of leaving licensing hearings until a new supermarket is almost ready to open.

- Recognise food labels from trusted overseas systems by default. Accept labels that meet UK, EU or US requirements, removing the need for New Zealand-specific packaging runs or item-by-item relabelling simply because the information is presented differently.
- Cut regulatory barriers to opening new stores. Remove unnecessary and inconsistent local requirements that add cost and delay when a supermarket wants to open in a new town.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“ACT would create a one-stop consenting shop for new market entrants - a single point where a business looking to open, or open multiple sites, can get their consents, their liquor licences, their approvals, in months, not years.

“ACT will allow food labels for trusted regulatory systems like UK, EU and US by default. This will lower the barrier to entry for international supermarkets, who will no longer need to do expensive runs of products specifically for the tiny Australasian market to open stores. ACT will roll out the welcome mat.
“Rather than joining the race to the bottom where we attack successful businesses, ACT’s policy is to make it easier for new businesses to come here, compete, and expand.”
####### Law & Order
## Crack Down on Noisy Vehicles
On some streets, loud exhausts and car stereos are a regular nuisance. Residents can report a noisy vehicle, but once it has gone, it’s hard to prove how loud it was.
Excessive vehicle noise is already against the law. ACT will make those rules easier to enforce in neighbourhoods where the problem keeps coming back.
Read ACT’s full policy, Crack Down on Noisy Vehicles, here.
#### ACT will:
- Introduce relocatable noise cameras that can be deployed in communities with persistent problems, collecting evidence when a noisy vehicle passes.
- Set enforceable roadside noise limits of 86 decibels on roads with speed limits of 50 km/h or less, and 90 decibels on roads with speed limits above 50 km/h and up to 70 km/h.
- Increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise, treating noise from equipment inside the vehicle consistently with noise from its engine or exhaust.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT's Tāmaki Candidate James Christmas says:
“Hard working Kiwis shouldn’t be punished by people who can’t take personal responsibility for their noise. Noise cameras enable evidence of offending to be collected the moment the offence occurs.
“Pairing technology with clear standards and real consequences will give residents the peace and quiet they deserve and ensure the comfort of many isn’t sacrificed for the noise of a few.”

## Make Farming Fun Again
A strong payout is welcome. What matters is what’s left after the bills are paid. Farming should offer the chance to get ahead and build a future for your family.
ACT will drive down farming costs and give farmers more freedom to farm. We’ll keep agricultural emissions untaxed and remove costly resource consents for routine work that meets clear standards.

ACT has already eased winter grazing rules and kept agriculture outside the ETS. Party Vote ACT to lock Labour out and unlock New Zealand’s potential, and give the next generation the freedom to farm.
Read ACT’s full plan to Make Farming Fun Again here.
### ACT will:
#### Drive down farming costs
- Keep agricultural emissions untaxed. Keep agriculture permanently out of the Emissions Trading Scheme and oppose any agricultural emissions tax or pricing scheme.
- Cut the carbon tax driving up the price of fuel and other farm inputs.
- Remove resource consent costs for routine farm work that meets clear national standards.
- Let farmers change what they farm without needing a resource consent where the change is consistent with National Standards.

- Make councils pay fair compensation when they restrict private land through overlays such as Significant Natural Areas or Outstanding Natural Landscapes. Protect farmers from a return to Labour-style Significant Natural Areas rules.

- Cut government waste and balance the books without new taxes. Return to surplus faster and pay down debt, helping ease pressure on inflation and interest rates. Keep the Reserve Bank focused on controlling inflation.
#### Give farmers the tools to grow
- Speed up access to proven agricultural chemicals and veterinary medicines by recognising trusted overseas approvals, reducing regulatory costs and improving access to competing products.
- Remove unnecessary restrictions on agricultural drones and other technology that can improve productivity and reduce operating costs.
- Introduce a Rural Workforce Visa and keep employment settings that make it easier for farms and rural businesses to recruit and employ staff.
- Cut red tape around homekill and make it easier for farmers to sell their products directly to consumers.
- Respect farmer-owned companies’ right to make commercial decisions without political interference.
#### Back rural families and communities
- Fund 100,000 additional rural Police patrol hours each year and establish a dedicated rural crime unit.
- Strengthen offences and penalties for livestock theft and poaching. Introduce Three Strikes for Burglary, with a minimum three-year prison sentence without parole on a third conviction.
- Increase penalties for illegal rubbish dumping, so farmers are less likely to be left with someone else’s clean-up bill.
- Allow rural children to use spare seats on existing school buses going to nearby schools wherever practical.
- Keep Agricultural and Horticultural Science as a standalone Year 11 subject.
- Strengthen vocational pathways into careers such as agriculture and horticulture.
- Expand everyday healthcare through pharmacies, including management of stable long-term conditions. Enable 24-hour prescription e-lockers, reducing travel and time away from the farm.
- Extend Text 111 eligibility to rural areas with unreliable voice coverage.
#### Back practical environmental work
- Commit to long-term funding to eradicate wilding pines, and direct DOC to coordinate pest control across public and private land, reducing the burden on individual farmers.
- Make permanent forest owners carry their forests’ long-term costs and risks, including sufficient pest control.
- Allow targeted grazing on suitable DOC land to control weeds and fire risk.
- Redirect $4.5 million a year within MPI to keep catchment-group funding at $13.5 million, allowing further funding where groups demonstrate strong water-quality results.
- Expand voluntary conservation through biodiversity credits and the QEII National Trust.
#### Set clear rules farmers can work with
- Put property rights first in the national rules under the new RMA laws. Focus on measurable environmental harm and local conditions, developing standards with farmers, growers and councils.

- Introduce at least ten new permitted activity standards covering farm plans, vegetable growing, on-farm water storage, gravel extraction, drain maintenance, effluent management, fertiliser application, farm quarries, wetland restoration, and small- and medium-scale solar. Activities meeting those standards won’t need a resource consent.
- Keep freshwater farm plans practical and affordable, with clear rules focused on actual environmental harm and local conditions.

- Require councils to use a science-based national method for setting freshwater limits, reflecting differences between catchments. Remove Te Mana o te Wai and other vague spiritual concepts, and prevent their return under another name.
- Strengthen property rights through the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
- Review the Sharemilking Agreements Act so it reflects how farming businesses operate today.
#### End costly climate policy
- Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and end the Net Zero target.
- Abolish the Climate Change Commission.
- Remove the artificial ETS price floor encouraging blanket carbon farming.
- Recognise methane’s different warming effect from carbon dioxide.
- Prevent international climate commitments imposing costs overseas competitors avoid. Reconsider the Paris Agreement if New Zealand cannot secure a fair deal.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Agriculture Spokesperson Andrew Hoggard says:

“There’s nothing fun about paperwork, especially when it’s pointless, yet farmers have been hit with endless new rules and freshwater regulations, Significant Natural Areas [SNAs], winter grazing, emissions pricing, the ute tax, firearms changes, health and safety paperwork, and resource management red tape. Successive governments piled on the rules, adding costs and uncertainty to running a farm.

“Farmers do not need another politician telling them how to farm. They need a Government that respects property rights, sets clear rules around genuine environmental harm, and otherwise lets them get on with it.”

####### Economy & Cost of Living
## Abundant and Affordable Electricity
Cheaper power puts more money in your pocket and gives businesses room to grow. New Zealand needs much more electricity, and people are ready to invest their own money in producing it.

Building and connecting new generation has been made unnecessarily difficult and slow. Households putting solar panels on their roofs face barriers to selling the power they make. Around a quarter of a typical power bill goes to a local lines monopoly you cannot switch away from.
ACT has already secured the repeal of Labour’s oil and gas ban. We need to lock Labour out and unlock New Zealand’s potential by backing the people ready to build more power.
Read our full policy, Stability, investment, affordability: The keys to abundant electricity, here.
#### ACT will:

- Let you choose who buys your power. Households could sell to a different provider from the one they buy electricity from, or through local businesses and community energy schemes, with proper metering, network charges and consumer protections.
- Lift unnecessary limits on your solar. Allow households to export more power where the network has room. Make lines companies explain and justify restrictions.

- Get new power connected faster. Let private investors build and operate their own transmission lines connected to the National Grid, meeting common technical and reliability standards. The generators and customers using those lines would pay through voluntary agreements.
- Let you shop around for a connection. Open eligible work on new or upgraded connections to competing accredited contractors. Lines companies would still set the safety and technical standards.

- Make lines companies prove an upgrade is worth it. Require them to test major upgrades against competing options, such as batteries or ways to reduce demand at peak times, before putting the cost on your bill.

- Keep investment in more power coming. Oppose forced break-ups of the major companies that generate and sell electricity. Strengthen enforcement when companies misuse market power to shut out competitors or block fair access to electricity markets and infrastructure.
- Cut red tape for solar power by implementing the recommendations of the Ministry for Regulation's Solar Regulatory Review, including legalising plug in solar.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Energy and Resources Spokesperson Simon Court says:

“New Zealand became a prosperous country in part because we were blessed with abundant energy. But you cannot maintain a first-world standard of living without reliable, affordable power. When energy becomes scarce and expensive, households feel it in their power bills, businesses face higher costs, investment becomes harder, and ultimately New Zealanders’ standard of living suffers.

“The answer is not for politicians to go looking for successful businesses to blame or promising to pull the electricity market apart. We’ve seen that before with the oil and gas ban. We need to make it easier for people to invest, generate more electricity, build the networks needed to move it, and compete for customers. That is how New Zealand gets abundant electricity and lower costs.”

## Backing Small Business
Small businesses turn hard work and good ideas into opportunities for other New Zealanders, from a first job to the higher wages that come with growth.
Every cost and stupid rule imposed by Government makes that growth harder, leaving workers with fewer opportunities and customers paying more.
ACT has already cut red tape for small businesses in Government. This package goes further so the people who build businesses and those who work for them can get ahead through their own effort.
Read ACT’s full policy, Let small business get on with business, here.
#### ACT will:
- Freeze the adult minimum wage for three years, giving employers certainty and allowing productivity to catch up with past increases.
- Introduce a Training Wage set at 60 per cent of the adult minimum wage for workers under 20 during their first 12 months with an employer.
- Allow employers and employees to begin protected negotiations about a consensual exit, while maintaining safeguards against coercion.

- Require personal grievance proceedings to be lodged with the Employment Relations Authority within three months of the grievance being raised, rather than leaving claims hanging over a business for up to three years.
- Make payroll deductions for union fees voluntary, so employers are not forced to collect fees on a union’s behalf. This policy was developed from a Member's Bill by ACT MP Parmjeet Parmar.
- Allow businesses to deduct productive software and digital investment under clear and consistent tax rules.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Small Business spokesperson Laura McClure says:
“New Zealand will not become more prosperous by making it harder to employ somebody, take a chance on a young worker, resolve a dispute, or invest in technology.

“ACT’s approach is different from the assumption that every problem needs another rule. New Zealanders have enormous potential when Government gets out of the way and allows them to get on with reaching it.

“Successful small businesses get more people in work, and create higher wages. Achieving that requires a dedicated presence in Government focused on unlocking the potential of every New Zealander willing to build, hire, innovate, and take risks.”

## An Easier End to Dead-End Employment
Small businesses shouldn’t need a lawyer just to have a difficult conversation about someone’s employment.

Sometimes an employment relationship is no longer working. An employer may be willing to pay the employee to leave, and the employee may be happy to accept. Under today’s law, simply raising that possibility can expose the business to a personal grievance.

ACT’s Golden Handshake policy would let both sides discuss a voluntary exit. The employee is free to say no. If they agree, the deal goes in writing and both sides can move on. ACT trusts adults to make their own decisions.
#### ACT will:
- Allow an employer to offer an employee a specified payment to end their employment by mutual agreement, whether or not a dispute has already arisen.
- Protect the employee’s right to reject the offer.
- Stop the offer itself from becoming grounds for a personal grievance.
- Generally keep the offer and resulting negotiations out of later Employment Relations Authority proceedings.
- Require every agreement to be written and signed by both sides.
- Require the employer to advise the employee to seek independent advice and give them a reasonable opportunity to do so.
- Make an accepted agreement a full and final settlement of claims arising from the employment relationship.
### In our team’s words:
ACT Small Business spokesperson Laura McClure says:
“In some cases, an employer would happily offer an employee compensation to leave, and the employee would happily accept. But current law makes it unnecessarily risky to even start that conversation.
“Small businesses shouldn’t need a lawyer just to have a difficult conversation.

“There is no reason our laws cannot treat people like adults and provide the opportunity to reach a fair agreement, shake hands, and move on before a difficult employment relationship turns into an expensive legal dispute.”
####### Democracy & Equal Rights
## Wind up the Waitangi Tribunal

The Waitangi Tribunal has made an important contribution to New Zealand. Its historical work helped identify Crown wrongdoing and created a pathway to resolve past injustices, including the confiscation of land and other breaches of property rights. Most historical claims have now been heard or settled. Those still outstanding should be completed properly.

But the modern Tribunal now passes judgement on day-to-day government policy, proposes alternative policy settings, and seeks to influence decisions that belong to elected Governments and Parliament. It should not operate as a parallel policy institution.

As New Zealand approaches 2040, two hundred years after the signing of the Treaty, it is time to finish the historical settlement process. Every New Zealander should have their rights protected through the same law and courts as we move forward under one law for all with one future together.
Read our full policy 'Finish the settlements, wind up the Waitangi Tribunal', here.
#### ACT will:

- Complete every eligible historical claim already before the Tribunal. Its jurisdiction will be limited to historical claims lodged by the existing statutory deadline of 1 September 2008, without rushing or cutting off genuine claimants.
- End the Tribunal’s jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, leaving it to focus solely on completing its remaining historical work.
- Strengthen property rights for every New Zealander by adding them to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act, so unlawful interference by the Crown can be challenged through the ordinary courts.
- Amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so the Tribunal is automatically disestablished once all eligible historical claims have been completed, rather than imposing an arbitrary closure date.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“The Waitangi Tribunal has been part of New Zealand’s constitutional landscape for more than fifty years. It has made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances. But no institution should exist just because it always has,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Every New Zealander deserves strong legal protections and access to the courts, regardless of ancestry. ACT believes those protections should be strengthened for everyone, not maintained through a permanent separate system for one group.

“As 2040 approaches, we should complete the remaining historical settlements, protecting every New Zealander’s right under the same law and courts, and move forward under one law for all with one future together.”

####### Rural
## Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax

New Zealand should play its part in reducing emissions. But a country responsible for just 0.17 per cent of global emissions needs a sense of proportion. There is no virtue in making petrol, power and food more expensive here while our major trading partners refuse to carry the same costs.

The Zero Carbon Act locks New Zealand into net zero by 2050, whatever our trading partners do. The Emissions Trading Scheme then adds a carbon cost to almost everything New Zealanders buy. At a carbon price of about $55, it costs an average household an estimated $478 a year.

ACT was the only party to vote against the Zero Carbon Act in 2019. We will repeal it, tie our emissions cap to what our trading partners are doing, remove the artificial auction price floor and return the revenue to New Zealanders. If the carbon price rises, the refund rises too.

A climate policy that closes a factory here so the same product can be made overseas has only exported jobs and emissions. Meanwhile, skewed carbon incentives are swallowing productive farms. ACT will give Kiwi industry and farming a fair go and let cleaner technology compete without needless red tape.
Read the full policy, Scrap Net Zero, Cut the Carbon Tax, here.
### ACT will
- Scrap the arbitrary net zero 2050 target and repeal the Zero Carbon Act.
- Tie New Zealand’s emissions cap to a trade-weighted average of our major trading partners.

- Cut the carbon tax by removing the Government’s artificial minimum price for carbon auctions. In 2026, the minimum was $71 while units were trading in the low $50s, contributing to six failed auctions in a row.
- Return 100 per cent of net carbon auction revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund. If the amount becomes too small for individual refunds, it will fund other tax relief.

- Protect Kiwi jobs where overseas competitors face lower or no carbon prices. Industrial carbon assistance will return to its original 90 and 60 per cent rates, with the automatic phase-down stopped while that disadvantage remains. Assistance of up to 100 per cent will be available in exceptional cases.

- Fix the rules that favour converting productive farmland to permanent carbon forests. Permanent forest owners will remain responsible for pest control and for the cost if stored carbon is later released.
- Cut red tape holding back cheaper, cleaner technology and oppose new climate taxes, including a tax on agricultural emissions.
- Renegotiate New Zealand’s commitment under the Paris Agreement. If a fairer arrangement cannot be reached, New Zealand should be prepared to leave.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealand’s climate policy is broken and sending the country broke as a result. A small trading nation can’t ignore climate policy, but overdoing it backfires and puts unnecessary costs on Kiwi businesses and households.
“ACT is the OG No New Taxes party, so we’ll return carbon auction revenue to taxpayers rather than giving politicians another pot of money to spend.”
ACT Climate Change spokesperson Simon Court says:
“If a New Zealand business can produce steel, cement, aluminium or food more efficiently than its overseas competitors, closing that business is an economic own goal and an environmental one too.
“Families are already paying too much at the supermarket and the last thing we should be doing is weakening our ability to grow food by turning productive farms into pine forests.”

## Keep New Zealand Moving

New Zealanders pay at the pump, through road-user charges, rates and tolls. They should see that money in reliable roads and shorter journeys. Instead, potholes go unfixed, new housing arrives before the roads needed to support it, and projects become slower and more expensive than they need to be.

ACT will put the basics first. We will build ahead of growth, maintain the network we already have, and stop transport money being diverted into vanity projects or procurement based on ethnicity. We will also stop unnecessary rules pricing families out of reliable vehicles.
New Zealand cannot unlock its potential while people and freight are stuck in traffic. ACT will build more, waste less and make every transport dollar deliver.
Read ACT’s full policy, Keep New Zealand Moving, here.
#### ACT will:
- Require major projects to publish the lowest-cost safe option alongside the preferred option, including the cost, delivery time and benefit-cost ratio of each.

- Build roads ahead of growth. On major two-lane growth corridors, 10,000 vehicles a day will trigger route protection, 15,000 will trigger consenting, design and a funded capacity plan, and 20,000 will trigger construction of additional lanes where growth continues.

- Require councils to repair potholes, drainage, and bridges before funding street redesigns, by protecting maintenance and renewal funding in the National Land Transport Fund so it cannot be raided for other projects.
- Make equal treatment a condition of Crown infrastructure funding. Ethnicity will not determine who can bid, how bids are scored, who receives preference or who must be subcontracted.
- Stop the National Land Transport Fund paying for non-functional art, monuments and decorative extras. Motorists’ money should build and maintain the transport network.
- Scrap unrealistic vehicle-emissions settings, oppose arbitrary age bans and require new rules to disclose their effect on vehicle supply and prices.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Infrastructure spokesperson Simon Court says:
"New Zealand does not need to accept deteriorating roads, unaffordable projects and congestion as the price of growth.
"The payoff for drivers and the public is more value from their every dollar with standard, proven designs and transparent published projects with their timelines.
"ACT will build more, waste less and make every transport dollar deliver, so New Zealand keeps moving."

## Put ‘Reside’ Back in ‘Resident’

New Zealand should welcome people who want to build a life here. But if someone wants the permanent right to return as a New Zealand resident, it is reasonable to expect them to maintain a real connection to the country.

Right now, someone can hold a Permanent Resident Visa without continuing to live in New Zealand. They can leave and re-enter indefinitely, leaving almost no practical distinction between permanent residence and citizenship.

ACT will put ‘reside’ back in ‘resident’. Residents will receive a five-year travel facility and will need to spend at least 730 days in New Zealand during any rolling five-year period to keep it. The days will not need to be continuous, and sensible exemptions will cover people working or serving New Zealand overseas, accompanying family members, and compelling humanitarian circumstances.
This policy is not retrospective – existing Permanent Resident Visa holders will not be affected. And exemptions for the Active Investor Plus Visa, also known as the Golden Visa, will remain.
#### ACT will:
- Remove the existing Permanent Resident Visa category.
- Give all Resident Visa holders a five-year travel facility, replacing the current two-year initial travel condition.
- Require Resident Visa holders to be physically present in New Zealand for at least 730 days within any rolling five-year period to maintain their travel facility.
- Allow the 730 days to be accumulated across the five years rather than requiring them to be continuous.
- Remove the indefinite, unconditional right to leave and re-enter New Zealand as a resident without maintaining an ongoing connection to the country.

- Provide exemptions for people working overseas for New Zealand employers, accompanying family members, military personnel serving overseas, people with a New Zealand citizen spouse, those with compelling humanitarian reasons, and holders of the Active Investor Plus Visa.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Immigration spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar says:
"The strangest immigration policy we have is that permanent residents don’t have to be permanently resident.
"New Zealand is, and should be, a welcoming country for migrants, but the privileges of permanent residence must reflect a real and lasting connection to our nation.

"This would also create a clearer answer to the question, what is the difference between permanent residence and citizenship? Right now, the two have nearly identical everyday rights. By introducing standard travel conditions, we create an evident distinction, giving people a reason to graduate to citizenship.

"To unlock New Zealand’s potential, there needs to be a balance between rights and responsibilities. ACT’s plan encourages migrants who choose to make New Zealand their permanent home to continue actively living and contributing here, while also ensuring a fair system for all taxpayers."
####### Democracy & Equal Rights
## No Votes for Unelected Reps

Your council spends your rates and decides what you can do with your property. You should be able to vote out every person who has a vote at the council table. ACT will remove voting rights from unelected appointees, including members of Auckland’s Independent Māori Statutory Board.

Councils across New Zealand have put appointees on committees alongside elected councillors. These appointees can swing a decision, but ratepayers have no way to remove them at an election. ACT will stop councils doing this.

In Auckland, two Houkura members of the Independent Māori Statutory Board vote on council committees dealing with natural and physical resource management. They hold those votes by appointment. ACT will remove those voting rights. Anyone who wants a vote at the council table can stand for election and ask Aucklanders for their support.
ACT stands for one law for all with one future together. If you want political power, you should stand for election like anyone else.
Read our announcement here.
#### ACT will:
- Change the Local Government Act so unelected members of council committees and subcommittees cannot vote or count toward quorum.
- Change the law governing Auckland Council so unelected members of the Independent Māori Statutory Board cannot vote on council committees.
- Apply the same rule to every appointee, whether they represent iwi, youth councils, business groups, or community organisations.
- Leave council decisions to the elected representatives ratepayers can vote out.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Local Government spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“With rates climbing and households squeezed, the people deciding how to spend ratepayers’ money ought to be held accountable. But right now, we’ve got councils appointing unelected people to committees with full voting rights.

“ACT’s coalition agreement has restored communities’ right to vote on Māori wards. But some councils may be tempted to counter a public vote against Māori wards by turning around and appointing unelected representatives anyway, along the lines of Auckland Council’s Independent Māori Statutory Board. Meanwhile, we’ve seen cases, such as in Tauranga and Wellington, where both Māori ward councillors and unelected mana whenua appointees sit across the same table.
“Ratepayers are struggling under rising bills. The only real accountability mechanism they have is the ballot box. If you’re paying the bills, you should be able to choose who’s spending your money".
####### Hunters and Firearms
## Plenty Is Possible

New Zealand should be one of the best places in the world to fish. Whether you make your living at sea or take the kids out on a Saturday, there should be more fish in the water and a fair chance of bringing something home.

Instead, too many fisheries are managed around scarcity. Local depletion can be hidden inside huge management areas, vulnerable coastlines can be stripped, and blunt rules can punish responsible fishers without stopping the real damage.

ACT believes plenty is possible. We will protect the resource without locking people out of it, rebuild fisheries where they are depleted, and manage important stocks for abundance rather than the bare minimum.
Read our full policy, Unlocking New Zealand’s Fishing Potential, here.
### ACT will:

- Restore abundance in the Hauraki Gulf. Establish a distinct fisheries management area matching the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park, so catch settings reflect what is actually happening within the Gulf instead of averaging it across a much larger area. Existing quota holders would keep their proportional property rights.

- Stop rock pools being stripped. Introduce a nationwide combined recreational daily bag limit of 10 for shellfish and other covered species that do not already have their own limit. Families could still gather a modest feed, but a small number of people could no longer strip an area bare.
- Keep scallop dredges out of closed fisheries. Permanently end dredging in currently closed North Island scallop fisheries and allow selective, lower-impact harvesting if stocks recover.

- Make fishing levies reflect the damage caused. Require Fisheries New Zealand to assess the environmental and economic costs of major harvesting methods, then rebalance existing levies without increasing the overall burden. Higher-impact methods would pay a greater share and lower-impact fishing would pay less.
- Make serious rule-breaking carry serious consequences. Increase and stagger infringement fees so minor breaches are treated differently from deliberate, repeat or large-scale offending.

- Aim for abundance, not survival. Stop treating maximum sustainable yield as the finish line. ACT will progressively manage important fisheries for larger fish populations, giving them room to withstand poor spawning years, changing conditions and mistakes in the science.
### In our team’s words:
ACT Conservation spokesperson Cameron Luxton says:

“Fishing puts food on New Zealand tables whether it is caught off the rocks or picked up with Friday night’s chips. It supports people who make their living at sea and is part of growing up in this country.
“We should not accept decline as normal. A system that aims to leave just enough fish in the water to sustain the maximum possible catch is setting the bar too low. ACT wants real abundance.

“A larger fish population gives us breathing room when spawning is poor or the science gets it wrong. It also means commercial crews spend less time and fuel finding their catch, while families have a better chance of bringing home dinner.

“New Zealanders do not have to choose between fishing and conservation. A healthy marine environment is what makes a successful fishing industry possible. The answer is to target the actual harm, protect vulnerable places and back responsible fishers."

## Unlocking New Zealand's Digital Economy
A Kiwi with a good idea should be able to build it here. Instead, our financial rules are still catching up with technology that is already changing how people raise money, invest and get paid.

A fintech start-up can face rules designed for major financial institutions before it has even proved its product. Legitimate digital-finance businesses can struggle to get a bank account. Someone making a small purchase with digital assets can face pointless tax paperwork. That holds New Zealand back.

ACT will modernise the rules so Kiwis can get investment into good ideas, build new financial businesses here and use new ways of moving money, without giving up strong protections against fraud and financial crime.
Read our full policy, Unlocking New Zealand's Digital Economy, here.
#### ACT will:
- Make international payments faster and cheaper. ACT will set clear rules for qualifying payment stablecoins, including strong requirements to protect consumers and the financial system.

- Stop pointless tax paperwork on small purchases. ACT will introduce a sensible exemption for low-value purchases made with digital assets, so Inland Revenue can focus on transactions that actually matter.

- Make it easier for New Zealand businesses to raise money. ACT will create clear legal and tax rules for tokenised assets, allowing ownership in things like businesses, farms, infrastructure and commercial property to be divided and transferred digitally with confidence.

- Give financial start-ups room to prove themselves. Innovative businesses will be able to test new products under supervision before being required to meet the full regulatory regime designed for established financial institutions.

- Give long-term digital investors a clear tax rule. Qualifying personal investments held for more than 12 months will fall outside the new bright-line rule. Professional traders and businesses will continue to be taxed under existing rules.
- Tackle blanket de-banking. ACT will review rules that may be encouraging banks and payment providers to shut legitimate, properly regulated fintech businesses out of essential financial services.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Deputy Leader Nicole McKee says:

“New technology is changing how businesses raise capital, how people invest, and how money moves around the world. Tokenised assets can open up new sources of investment. Stablecoins can make international payments faster and cheaper. New financial technology can create high-value businesses and jobs.

“ACT will cut red tape, set clear rules, and open up investment so Kiwis can raise capital, pay and get paid more easily, and take part in the technologies shaping the future - while keeping strong consumer and financial safeguards".
ACT MP Cameron Luxton says:
“ACT will be unlocking more growth, better jobs, and a future-ready economy that New Zealanders can participate in.
"We will align digital finance policy with a bigger goal, getting capital flowing to good ideas and helping entrepreneurs build globally competitive businesses from New Zealand."

## Scrap the Climate Change Commission

While New Zealanders are watching every dollar, Wellington has already spent $100 million on the Climate Change Commission and keeps handing it another $14–15 million a year to produce reports that duplicate work already being done in government or recommend policies that harm the country.

Those recommendations are not harmless paperwork. One proposal to tighten the 2050 emissions target would make the economy 2.2 per cent smaller, costing New Zealanders $2 billion a year by 2035 and $12.5 billion every year by 2050. The Commission has also proposed shrinking New Zealand’s dairy herd, punishing some of the world’s most emissions-efficient farmers and risking production moving to dirtier countries.

ACT will abolish the Commission and transfer its monitoring and reporting duties to the ministry that already measures New Zealand’s emissions and manages the Emissions Trading Scheme. New Zealand does not need two climate bureaucracies charging taxpayers for the same job.
#### ACT will:
- Abolish the Climate Change Commission as an independent Crown entity. The Commission will cease to exist.
- Transfer responsibility for monitoring and reporting on New Zealand’s emissions targets to the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport.
- Bring emissions monitoring together with the greenhouse gas inventory and the Emissions Trading Scheme, so one department is responsible for the work.
- End the Commission’s separate role recommending costly new targets and interventions such as shrinking New Zealand’s dairy herd.
- Remove the Commission’s board, executive and corporate overhead, ending the need for taxpayers to support a separate $14–15 million-a-year climate bureaucracy.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Candidate Paul Henry says:

"The Climate Change Commission has cost taxpayers $100 million since its establishment, and is costing a further $14–15 million every year it continues to exist. Left in place, that's another $42–45 million of taxpayer money gone by the next election spent on writing reports, duplicating work, and proposing ludicrous ideas that will be ignored.

"Their barking mad recommendation to increase our 2050 emissions reduction commitment would have lowered GDP by 2.2%. That’s around $2 billion a year by 2035, rising to about $12.5 billion every year by 2050, wiped from our economy to meet an arbitrary target.

"They put up proposals even Labour and the Greens can’t get behind. In the last term of Government they recommended tighter Emissions Trading Scheme restrictions, but Cabinet rejected it. Commission-linked advice supported a 54% net reduction for the 2030 emissions reduction pledge, but Cabinet opted for a 50% reduction instead. Even the left could recognise a stupid idea.

"We can’t afford to see taxpayer dollars blown on inefficient government agencies and counterproductive climate policies. To unlock New Zealand’s potential and make life more affordable, the waste and duplication need to go. Go sell stupid somewhere else, we’re all full up here."
####### Health
## A Starship for Cancer

Cancer is New Zealand’s biggest killer. More than 30,000 New Zealanders are diagnosed each year, and around 1,000 more die from cancer each year than would if our cancer mortality rate matched Australia’s.

New Zealanders should not have to accept second-rate cancer care. Starship showed what can happen when we bring our best people, technology, research and generosity together. ACT wants to do the same for cancer.

ACT will support a world-class National Cancer Centre with campuses in Auckland and Christchurch. It will bring complex treatment, research, clinical trials and specialist expertise together in one institution. We want New Zealand to have cancer care that stands alongside the best in the world.
Read ACT's full policy, Beyond Tomorrow – A Starship for Cancer, here.
#### ACT will:
- Build National Cancer Centre campuses in Auckland and Christchurch.
- Bring cancer treatment, research, clinical trials, and specialist expertise together in world-class centres.
- Establish an independent National Cancer Centre Foundation to attract major philanthropic investment.
- Use public-private partnerships, philanthropy, existing health investment, and private capital to fund the centres.
- Locate Health New Zealand’s relevant Auckland and Christchurch cancer services at the new centres.
- Remove the $33,333 cap on tax benefits for charitable donations.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Candidate Paul Henry says:
"I’ve joined politics because I am ambitious for New Zealand and think it has endless potential. We should not accept being second-rate at treating a disease that touches almost every family.
"Starship showed what New Zealand can achieve when we concentrate talent, technology, generosity and national ambition around a single mission. ACT wants to do the same for cancer.

"This is an investment in New Zealand’s future. It is the type of project that makes New Zealand the envy of the world and attracts private healthcare investment, new technologies and therapies, teaching, medical research, and international clinical trials."

blocks: ####### Law & Order
####### Education
## Keeping Children Safe

Parents should be able to send their child to school, sport or a youth group knowing the adults in charge are safe to be there. The current system can leave three years between checks, even if worrying new Police information emerges in the meantime.

ACT will close that gap with one national card checked continuously. If someone is charged with a serious offence that could rule them out of working with children, their card can be suspended immediately. They must stop working with children while the case is assessed, and their employer will be told.
Read ACT’s full policy, Keeping Children Safe, here.
#### ACT will:
- Create one national card that paid workers and volunteers must have to be able to work with children. It will belong to them and last three years.
- Keep people convicted of specified serious offences against children out of covered roles.

- Keep checking cardholders against new Police information. If Police learn someone may be dangerous, their card can be suspended. That means they cannot keep working with children, and every linked organisation will be told.
- Give every cardholder practical child-protection training, refreshed when the card is renewed.
- Keep applications exempt or discounted for volunteers and students. Paid workers will pay about $108, which employers will often cover.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT’s Children spokesperson Karen Chhour says:
“Parents should be able to leave their children with a teacher, coach, afterschool carer, or volunteer knowing the adults around them are safe to work with children.

“The current system does not provide that reassurance. Safety checks are carried out by individual employers and generally only re-checked every three years. This provides only a snapshot of a person at one point in time, with no consistent system for identifying risks that emerge between checks.
“The Working with Children Card gives parents peace of mind about their child’s safety, and creates a smarter, less burdensome screening process for employers and workers.”
####### Education
####### Economy & Cost of Living
## Real Choice for Students
ACT will campaign to make Student Services Fees voluntary – a move that would offer students real cost relief and ensure they are not forced to fund union activity.

Every domestic university student currently pays a compulsory Student Services Fee of up to $1,253 a year on top of tuition. Across a three-year degree this can add more than $4,000 to a student’s loan*. Because student loans are subsidised by the taxpayer, the compulsory fee also costs the taxpayer.
#### ACT will:

- ACT will amend the regulations so universities must offer student services as a menu. Students would select the services they want and pay only for those, from fitness facilities to students unions and student media. Services not chosen would still be available on a transparent user-pays basis.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Tertiary Education spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar says:
“Students should not be forced to fund unions, advocacy or student media they do not support. That is a matter of principle for ACT.

“Right now, student unions are running political campaigns to influence the election. They might even campaign to stop this policy. Students are forced to fund this activism, even if they disagree with it. ACT says unions are free to campaign, but no-one should be forced to fund them.

“Our policy would let students save up to around $4,000 on their student loan over the course of a degree. It would also save the taxpayer money, because student debt is subsidised. We will complete the unfinished business of Voluntary Student Membership and restore genuine choice.”
*After annual increases to the fee.

blocks: ####### Rural
## Grazing to Cut Pests and Fire Risk

“Taxpayers are footing the bill for a helicopter spraying programme when a flock of sheep could be doing the job for free,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard as he releases new rural policy at Fieldays.
ACT will:

- Amend the Conservation Act 1987: ACT will give DOC explicit authority and direction to issue grazing licences for specified areas of conservation land where grazing supports vegetation management objectives.

- Target invasive plants and fire risk: ACT will establish a clear ecological framework to identify where grazing is appropriate to suppress conifer seedlings and other invasive vegetation, while reducing the fuel loads that contribute to devastating wildfires.

- Set practical licence conditions: ACT will ensure licences specify appropriate stocking types, rates, and duration, ensuring the land is managed effectively without burying farmers in bureaucratic red tape.
- Allow virtual fencing: ACT will recognise virtual fencing systems as a compliant method of stock exclusion to reduce the burden on farmers grazing their stock on DOC land.
#### In our team’s words:

“Taxpayers are footing the bill for a helicopter spraying programme when a flock of sheep could be doing the job for free,” says ACT’s Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard as he releases new rural policy at Fieldays.

"Wilding conifers are the largest invasive species challenge in New Zealand, choking 1.8 million hectares of land. The Government has invested sensibly into fighting them, but we can do a lot more by allowing farmers to graze livestock.

"DOC manages large areas of open country, former pastoral land, and other nonforest conservation land that could be safely grazed under controlled conditions. Too often, however, farmers seeking grazing concessions are met with resistance or unnecessary barriers. The result is less active land management, more wilding pines, and growing fuel loads that increase wildfire risk.

"By locking up the land and throwing away the key, the Government hasn’t just allowed invasive plants and pests to thrive; it has turned parts of the conservation estate into a severe wildfire risk. The heavy vegetation fuel loads left behind are a disaster waiting to happen.

"The current rules make it unnecessarily difficult to use targeted grazing on Crown conservation land. Instead, taxpayers are forced to pay for expensive aerial spraying and manual cutting. It is a regulatory failure that is actively harming the environment and wasting public money.

"Overseas, they know better. In the United States, Australia, and across Europe, targeted grazing is a standard, internationally recognised tool for managing invasive plants, controlling vegetation growth, and reducing wildfire fuel loads. Portugal even uses it specifically to build forest resilience against fires. It’s time New Zealand caught up. It’s time to stop treating farmers like the enemy and start treating them as part of the solution. We need to unleash practical, rural knowledge on this crisis.”
####### Rural
####### Immigration
## A Rural Workforce Visa

ACT is announcing its new Rural Workforce Visa (RWV) policy, a dedicated pathway designed to give farmers a reliable, year-round pipeline of workers – without the visa uncertainty that leaves roles unfilled for months at a time.
ACT will:
- Create the Rural Workforce Visa: A standalone, three-year visa specifically for dairy, sheep and beef, and general farm work.

- Implement sector-tying, not geographic borders: The visa is attached to accredited rural employers, not a region. Workers can transfer to any other accredited rural employer without a new application, but cannot move to nonrural sectors. Workers end up in rural communities as a market outcome, not because a bureaucrat drew a line on a map.

- Cut bureaucracy: The visa features an initial three-year term with no renewal required within that period. Before the visa term ends, employers readvertise; if no suitable New Zealander is available, the visa is reissued for a further three years. This removes the repeated annual compliance load on employers.

- Establish a clear residency pathway: ACT will add a new agricultural stream to the Work to Residence Visa. Workers who have held an RWV for 72 cumulative months (six years) with an accredited employer, and who meet standard requirements, will become eligible for residence.
#### In our team’s words:

“New Zealand's farms, orchards, and fishing fleets generate $60 billion in exports every year. Right now, they can't find enough capable workers to do the job, held back by a chronic labour shortage that the current immigration system simply isn't equipped to solve," says ACT's Agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard.

“Rural New Zealand faces different pressures from urban New Zealand. In many communities, the problem isn't too many people arriving, it's not enough workers being available. Applying an infrastructure levy in those circumstances would make no sense, which is why ACT’s Rural Workforce Visa would be exempt. Federated Farmers’ latest Farm Confidence Survey confirms labour availability remains one of the biggest challenges facing farmers across the country.

“The Government has made progress by introducing the Global Workforce Seasonal Visa and Peak Seasonal Visa. Those pathways help meet seasonal demand, but they do not address the year round roles that keep farms running every day.

“Labour shortages don't just make it harder to run farms. They also make it harder to keep productive land in farming at a time when many rural communities are already under pressure from the expansion of forestry.”

“Immigration should support the industries that drive New Zealand's economy, not leave critical jobs sitting vacant. ACT's Rural Workforce Visa provides certainty and a straightforward pathway for reliable migrant workers to fill genuine workforce shortages. Our immigration settings should support the people who feed the country and drive our economy, not bury them in red tape.” says ACT’s Immigration spokesperson Dr Parmjeet Parmar.

Mr Hoggard says the policy respects the basic bargain that New Zealand was built on. People are welcome here if they contribute, respect our democratic values, and help build the country. It is a targeted, pro-market solution that rewards workers who have demonstrated sustained commitment to rural New Zealand.

“ACT’s Rural Workforce Visa reduces regulatory burdens on farmers, removes geographic restrictions, and delivers year-round workforce stability our primary industries need to drive New Zealand’s export economy forward,” says Mr Hoggard.
####### Democracy & Equal Rights
## One Public Service for All

ACT has already directed agencies to deliver services based on need, not identity. We have also strengthened the Public Service Act: public servants must stay politically neutral and appointments must be made on merit. But previous governments spent years building separate tracks for different groups, and too many of those rules remain.

ACT will remove them and build one public service with one standard for everyone that delivers help where it is needed and keeps public servants focused on the New Zealanders they serve. The same rules will apply, whoever you are.
Read ACT's full policy, One Public Service for All, here.
#### ACT will:

- End race-based hiring. Government jobs should go to the best candidate, whoever they are. But the law still tells public employers to shape employment policies around the aspirations and employment needs of particular ethnic groups. ACT will repeal those rules in section 73 of the Public Service Act and section 118 of the Crown Entities Act. Laws against discrimination and unsafe workplaces will remain. So will the rule that public service appointments must be based on merit.

- Deliver public services based on need, not race. ACT will put into law that public services should go to the people who need them, whoever they are. If two New Zealanders have the same need, government should treat them the same. The Government has already told agencies to follow that rule. ACT will put it in law so people can challenge decisions that break it in court.

- Keep spiritual practices voluntary. Taxpayer money isn't for running spiritual or religious activities at work. ACT will end the use of public time and public funds for this, whatever the tradition. Staff will remain free to practise their own religion, culture, or traditions in their own time, and workplaces can make reasonable arrangements for them.

- Remove cultural tests that have nothing to do with the job. Job ads should ask whether you can do the work, not whether you know the right cultural concepts or share the right worldview. ACT will tell agencies to remove these requirements from job ads and position descriptions unless the knowledge is actually needed for the job.

- Rewrite the Public Service Act. ACT will make these changes straight away, then rewrite the Act so the public service stays politically neutral, hires on merit, treats people equally, and is judged on whether services actually reach the people who need them.
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

"To unlock New Zealand's potential we need one law for all, and one future together. That starts with a public service that treats people as individuals, hires the best people for the job, and delivers services according to need.
"Public service jobs should go to the best person for the job, regardless of race. Hiring and promotion should be based on merit, skills, experience, and what the role actually requires.
"If two New Zealanders have the same need, they should be entitled to the same treatment from government.
"Nobody should be expected to take part in a prayer, karakia, or other spiritual practice because they work for the Government.
“ACT will ensure a public service capable of unlocking the potential of all New Zealanders. It will be neutral, professional, focused on results, and treat every person as an individual."
####### Health
## Let Pharmacies Do More
Someone with an ear infection should not have to wait a week to see a GP when a pharmacist can safely treat it.

One in four adults says the time taken to get an appointment was a barrier to seeing a GP. At the same time, New Zealand has more than a thousand community pharmacies staffed by qualified health professionals whose skills are not being fully used.
Pharmacists can already treat several common conditions. ACT would widen that list and set clear rules for when a patient needs to see a doctor.
#### ACT will:

- Let pharmacies treat more everyday conditions, including chest infections, ear infections, skin infections, acute pain, sore throats, tonsillitis, school sores, styes, gout, osteoarthritis, vaginal thrush and period pain, as well as provide STI self-swab testing.

- Allow accredited pharmacists to monitor stable hypertension, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol, and adjust medication within GP-set limits. Pharmacists could also order appropriate blood tests when requested or clinically necessary. GPs would retain overall clinical responsibility and visibility, with results recorded in the shared health record.

- Pilot pharmacy-based skin-lesion checks to help detect skin cancer sooner. Trained pharmacists would use dermatoscopes and an approved AI risk-assessment tool, with clear pathways for referral and monitoring.
- Remove barriers preventing new pharmacies from opening, including the five-pharmacy ownership cap and proximity restrictions, while cutting licensing red tape.
- Enable secure 24-hour prescription lockers so patients can collect eligible medicines when it suits them.
Read the full policy
#### In our team's words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:
“New Zealand is not short of medical expertise. The problem is access. GPs have long waiting lists, emergency departments are under pressure, and too many patients are stuck waiting for routine care.

“Pharmacists are trained health professionals, yet we still make them refer people back to a GP for conditions they could safely treat. If your pharmacist can sort it out, you should not have to join the GP queue.
“More than 120,000 people used the Minor Health Conditions Service pilot in 2023, and 88 per cent had their needs met at a pharmacy. We already know this model can work here.”
####### Economy & Cost of Living
####### Democracy & Equal Rights
## A Smaller, More Affordable Government
Making New Zealand affordable again must start at the top.

New Zealand has 78 ministerial portfolios, 28 ministers, and 43 departments. Norway has a similar population and runs with 20 ministers across 17 ministries. New Zealand’s oversized Government isn’t intentional, it’s like a hedge that stopped being trimmed years ago.
#### Under ACT’s plan:
- The 43 departments would be consolidated into 19 coherent departments.
- The 78 overlapping portfolios with 28 ministers would be collapsed into just 18 ministers.
- Each department would report to one minister for its budget and outcomes.*
- Ministers would be allowed to appoint chief executives for a fixed term, renewable once, with clear protections for officials.

- Chief executives could be removed by Ministers for specified reasons such as non-performance or policy misalignment, but they would retain public service protections and the right to return to a lower classified role.
- Operational independence would be protected by law for agencies that need it, such as Police, NZSIS, and NZDF.
ACT’s full proposal, ' ACT’s plan for a consolidated bureaucracy', can be found here.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:
“New Zealand needs a smaller, more efficient government if we are going to balance the books, lift wages, restore trust in democracy, and unlock New Zealand’s potential.

“The Government is too tangled to act. Housing, infrastructure, welfare dependency, crime, and health all cut across multiple agencies. When seven departments share a problem, it can stop being anyone’s job to solve it. Kiwis are left frustrated, bouncing between departments or denied straight answers.

“Sprawling, tangled bureaucracy is expensive. It costs money that can’t be returned to taxpayers, can’t pay down debt, can’t reach the nurse, teacher or police officer on the frontline, and can’t build the infrastructure we need.

“Overseas research shows more ministers with spending power means bigger deficits. When many ministers each control part of the budget, but the cost falls on the whole tax base, each has an incentive to grow their own spending while bearing only a fraction of the cost.
“ACT’s plan won’t affect frontline services like nurses, teachers, or police. If anything, it will make them more effective with clear lines of responsibility and a focus on their core role.

“The Coalition Government has accepted the argument for a smaller Government, but current changes are tinkering around the edges. Kiwis are tired of piecemeal change that takes forever, so ACT is proposing a thought-out plan for the whole government, that we can start rolling out immediately in the next term.

“ACT would also fix the broken accountability line between ministers and departmental chief executives. At the moment, ministers are held responsible for delivery, but they do not appoint the person leading the department responsible for that delivery. ACT would remove the Public Service Commission and allow ministers to appoint chief executives, and chief executives could be removed for specified reasons.

“That is how we unlock New Zealand’s potential. A government with clear structure and limits, not the tangled result of accidental growth. Small enough to be accountable, simple enough to act, and focused on results for New Zealanders instead of managing itself.”

## Welfare as a Hand Up, not a Way of Life
Welfare should unlock potential, not trap it. So why are we paying people to stay at home who could be doing jobs we are currently filling with migrants?
ACT’s welfare policy has two planks:
#### Tightening medical certification for health-related benefits

- All health and disability benefits will be independently issued by an MSD-approved pool of designated doctors.* A person’s usual GP or specialist will still be able to provide medical history, clinical notes, and supporting evidence.
- Assessments will be made against clear, objective criteria, rather than leaving major long-term benefit decisions to discretion.
- Existing Jobseeker Support – Health Condition or Disability and Supported Living Payment recipients will be reassessed against the new criteria on a phased basis.
- Reassessment will begin with mental-health-related grants made after the pandemic, where much of the recent growth has occurred.
- ACT will allow for long-term arrangements for those with a genuine, enduring disability or health condition so support stays in place for those who truly need it.
* The Government has already established this as an option, but ACT will make it mandatory.
#### Managed assistance for long-term Jobseeker recipients
- ACT will introduce electronic money management for Jobseeker Support Work Ready recipients who remain on a benefit for more than four months.*
- Their benefit will be delivered through an electronic payment card directed to essentials such as groceries, rent, power, transport, health and childcare.
- The card will block spending on alcohol, gambling, tobacco, and cash withdrawals.
- ACT will include carve-outs and modified arrangements where money management would risk safety or block access to necessities.
* New Zealand already has money management as an option in certain circumstances, but ACT will make it mandatory after the four-month threshold.
#### In our team’s words:
ACT Leader David Seymour says:

“New Zealanders believe in helping people through tough times. But the deal has to be fair: if you can work, you should be taking real steps toward work, and taxpayer support should go to the essentials it was intended to fund.

“Nobody should be denied support when they genuinely cannot work. But the public deserves confidence that the system is not being gamed, and that people are not being written off when work or greater independence is possible.

“Electronic money management means taxpayer support will not fund purchases that make it harder for people to get their lives back on track. If someone is receiving a benefit funded by working New Zealanders, that support should go to food, housing, power, transport, health, and childcare – not alcohol, gambling, or tobacco.

“Unlocking New Zealand’s potential means unlocking the potential of New Zealanders. That starts with a welfare system that backs people to move forward, rewards effort, protects taxpayers, and refuses to write people off."

try’s first Review of the End of Life Choice Act 2019 was published in November
2024 and made 25 substantial recommendations and various minor recommended
changes to improve the operation of the Act. These recommendations are organised
into 5 areas:
•     supporting access and safety:
•     improving the process to receive assisted dying:
•     aligning the Act with the wider health system:
•     ensuring a capable and effective workforce for assisted dying:
•     clarifying organisational roles and responsibilities in the Act.
Government parties agreed that any changes to the Act will be proposed through
members’ bills. This Bill amends the Act to give effect to all of the recommendations
made by the Ministry.
The Bill also makes additional amendments to the Act to reflect Australian and Cana‐
dian law, given the close alignment between Australian, Canadian, and New Zealand
legal and medical frameworks, and new evidence that has emerged since the Act was
enacted in 2019.
In 2024, the Australian Capital Territory Parliament passed the Voluntary Assisted
Dying Act 2024, which does not include a temporal requirement. The Canadian med‐

                  dying law to allow for a person who has met eligibility criteria to waive final consent
                  if they lose capacity in the period between choosing a date and time for administra‐
                  tion of medication and the date of administration. This change was informed by evi‐
                  dence from over five years of experience with medical assistance in dying in Canada,
                  feedback from over 300,000 public submissions, and the testimony of over 120 expert
                  witnesses.

                  cent of New Zealanders are in favour of removing the temporal requirement and
                  allowing a waiver of final consent, with the next greatest proportion being neutral or
                  unsure.

                  tions—

                         ing being aged 18 years or older, being in an advanced state of irreversible
                         decline in physical capability, experiencing unbearable suffering that cannot be
                         tolerably relieved, and being competent to make an informed decision about
                         assisted dying; and
                  •      introducing a limited waiver of final consent provision that will be available if
                         a person has capacity when making a request for assisted dying, being exam‐
                         ined and found eligible by medical practitioners, and choosing the date and
                         time for the assisted death, but loses capacity before the day of the assisted

                                   Advance Directives Bill
                                              Member's Bill

                                         Explanatory note

                                       General policy statement

This Bill establishes a clear legal framework for advance directives in New Zealand's health system.
An advance directive regulated by this Bill is a written document made by a person while they have
decision-making capacity that sets out their instructions or preferences about health treatment to apply
if they later lack capacity.

The Law Commission has recently observed that, in New Zealand, there is ongoing uncertainty about
both the requirements for making a valid advance directive and the circumstances in which health
practitioners are legally required to give effect to an advance directive. This uncertainty has
contributed to inconsistent understanding and application of advance directives by health practitioners.
The Law Commission has stated that these uncertainties could be addressed through clearer statutory
codification of the law. Similarly, the Health Committee, in an August 2025 review of advance
directives, concluded that deficiencies in the current advance directive framework warrant urgent
reform, including the establishment of a nationwide register of advance directives.

Further, comparable jurisdictions such as Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom have enacted
legislation governing advance directives, that define validity and applicability and provide protections
for health practitioners acting in accordance with advance directives. This statutory clarity promotes
more consistent clinical decision-making and gives both patients and practitioners clearer guidance on
when advance directives must be followed and when departure is permitted.

The purpose of the Bill is to protect the rights of patients to make informed decisions about their health
treatment by codifying the requirements for a valid advance directive and improving the ability of
health practitioners to provide care that respects those directives. It does this by setting out
requirements for making a valid advance directive, including witnessing and capacity standards,
creating a national register of advance directives and appointing a Registrar of Advance Directives to
maintain it. The register will enable health practitioners to quickly determine whether a person under
their care has an advance directive and the Bill will require practitioners to act consistently with any
advance directive identified through the register.

The Bill includes safeguards for privacy and access to information, clarifies the circumstances in which
departure from an advance directive is permitted, provides protection from liability for health
practitioners who rely in good faith on an advance directive, and clarifies the relationship between
advance directives and the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988. It also creates
offences relating to dishonesty or undue influence in the making or management of advance
directives, unauthorised creation, alteration or destruction of advance directives, knowingly making




3475-0158-0616
 false or misleading statements about advance directives, and wilful non‑compliance with the Act by
health practitioners.

Directives not recorded on the register will remain valid under the common law and the Code of Health
and Disability Services Consumers’ Rights. Similarly, advance mental health directives are excluded
from the scope of this Bill, as they are already expressly provided for under the Mental Health Bill.

The Bill is intended to promote personal autonomy, reduce uncertainty for health practitioners, patients
and their families, and ensure that people's treatment choices are recognised and respected across
the health system.

Clause 1 is the Title clause.

Clause 2 is the commencement clause. It provides that the Bill comes into force 6 months after Royal

                                  Duties of health practitioners

Clause 28 requires health practitioners to make all reasonable efforts to assess decision-making
capacity and identify registered advance directives before providing treatment, sets out obligations
relating to binding consent, refusals, and preferences and values, and specifies circumstances in
which departure from a registered advance directive is permitted.

Clause 29 requires health practitioners to report to the Registrar, as soon as practicable, whenever a
registered advance directive is followed or not followed, including the reasons if it was not followed
and whether this resulted in the person’s death.

Clause 30 provides for the rights of health practitioners to conscientiously object to providing,
withholding, or withdrawing treatment, subject to notification duties and ensuring another health
professional is available to provide the treatment to that person.

Clause 31 provides protection from civil, criminal and professional liability for health practitioners who,
in good faith, withhold or withdraw treatment in reliance on a registered advance directive.

Clause 32 provides immunity from liability for emergency treatment provided in circumstances where a
health practitioner is unaware of a refusal to treatment in an advance directive.

Clause 33 enables applications to the Family Court to resolve disputes or uncertainty about advance
directives.

directives.

Clause 36 creates an offence for knowingly making false or misleading statements about an advance
directive.

Clause 37 creates an offence for wilful non‑compliance with the Bill by health practitioners.

6            Meaning of advance directive

(1)          An advance directive is a document that sets out a person's (A) binding instructions or
             preferences and values in respect of 1 or more of the following matters to take effect in the

                      outcomes.

(2)          An advance directive may be given so as to apply—

             (a)      in all circumstances; or

             (b)      only in specified circumstances; or

             (c)      in all circumstances except in specified circumstances.

             (a)      at the time of making it, A has the capacity—

                                in respect of matters relating to their health and welfare; and

                      (ii)      to communicate decisions in respect of those matters; and

             (b)      it is made voluntarily, free from undue influence or coercion, and free from
                      improper pressure from any other person; and

             (c)      it is in writing and signed by A; and

             (d)      it is witnessed by a prescribed person; and

             (e)      the witness certifies in writing that, in the witness's opinion, the person making the
                      directive has the capacity referred to in paragraph (a).
